questionText:
An 18 year old young male comes in surgery OPD with sudden pain over scrotal region with history of vomiting. Pain increases on lifting testis. The most probable diagnosis is:
a. Acute epididymo-orchitis
b. Testicular torsion
c. Inguinal hernia
d. Hydrocele
explanation:
Intravaginal Testicular torsion:
Torsion occurs within the space of tunica vaginalis, which is highly invested
MC age :10-25 years, with peak in prepubertal age
Cremaster fibers have a spiral attachment over the cord, it favors rotation when cremaster reflex is strong

Predisposition Factors
Inversion of the testis (testis lies transversely or upside down) is MC predisposing factor
High investment of tunica vaginalis(clapper in a bell)
Separation of the epididymis from the body of testis

C/Fs
Sudden agonizing scrotal pain with nausea or vomiting
Dysuria or other bladder symptoms are usually absent
Affected testis high-riding in scrotum, may have abnormal transverse orientation
Cord is usually thickened
Absent cremasteric reflex is highly suggestive of torsion testis (present in epididymitis).
After several hours massive scrotal edema may obliterate all the findings
Prehn's sign is negative (On elevation of testis, pain relieved in epididymoorchitis but not in torsion testis)
Deming sign: Affected testis is at higher level because of twisting of cord
Angel sign: Opposite testis lies horizontally because of presence of mesorchium

Imaging
Color Doppler detects the decreased blood flow to testis in torsion and is IOC to exclude torsion in epididymoorchitis

Treatment
It is urological emergency
Immediate surgical exploration, because if treated within first 4 hours, chances of testicular salvage are high
Viable as well as testis of marginal viability are preserved and orchiopexy is done either by placing into dartos pouch without suture fixation or suture fixation of tunica albuginea with the parietal wall.
Exploration of contralateral hemiscrotum must be done. In almost all cases, a bell clapper deformity is found.
Contralateral testis must be fixed to prevent subsequent torsion.
Ref. Surgery Essence by Pritesh Singh 6/e pg. 666

Testicular torsion is most common between 10 to 25 years of age, although a few cases occur in infants. Typically, there is sudden agonizing pain in the groin or the lower abdomen. The patient feels nauseated and may vomit. Redness of the skin and a mild pyrexia may result in the condition being confused with epididymo-orchitis in the older patient; however, in epididymo-orchitis there will usually be dysuria associated with the accompanying urinary infection. Elevation of the testis reduces the pain in epididymo-orchitis and makes it worse in torsion.

Imp signs in Torsion of Testis:
- Prehn sign (Elevation of scrotum increases pain in torsion, relieves pain in epididymo-orchitis),
- Deming's sign (high riding testis tender near Superficial Inguinal Ring),
- Angell's sign (Opp testis lies horizontal).
- Rocher's Sign: A clinical sign which helps in differentiation of epididymitis from torsion of the testis. In torsion testes, the epididymis cannot be distinguished from the body of testes, whereas in epididymitis the body of testes can be felt in the enlarged crescent of epididymis.

questionText:
Peyronie's Disease affects:
a. Testis
b. Penis
c. Spleen
d. Thymus
explanation:
Peyronie's Disease are hard plaques of fibrosis in the tunica of one or both corpora cavernosa of penis. Erect penis bends towards the side of the plaque. It is associated with history of past trauma and Dupuytren's Contracture.
Peyronie's disease (plastic induration of penis / penile fibromatosis) usually seen over 40 years of age.
It is due to fibrous plaques in one or both corpus cavernosum of varying sizes involving tunica albuginea which may later calcify or ossify.
Cause remains obscure, the dense fibrous plaque is microscopically consistent with findings of severe vasculitis.
Palmar fibromatosis (Dupuytren's contracture), plantar fibromatosis and penile fibromatosis (Peyronie's disease) are components of the same pathological process called superficial fibromatosis.

Clinical features
- Painful erection, curvature of penis and poor erection distal to involved area.
- No pain when the penis is in nonerect state.
- Palpable induration or mass appears usually on the dorsolateral aspect of the penis.

Treatment
- Spontaneous remission occurs in about 50% cases, so observation and emotional support advised initially.
- If the penile deformity is distressing, Nesbitt's operation can be performed to straighten the penis.
- Nesbitt operation: Straightening of penis by placing non-absorbable sutures in corpus cavernosum opposite to the plaque.

questionText:
Not true about Peyronie's disease:
a. Self-limiting
b. Very aggressive
c. Fibrosis
d. Seen in penis
explanation:
Peyronie disease
Definition: fibroproliferative disorder that affects the tunica albuginea of the penis, causing abnormal curvature of the penis
Pathogenesis: repeated penile microtrauma during sexual intercourse or athletic activity followed by abnormal wound healing → fibrous plaque formation

Classification
- Active phase
  - Acute or inflammatory phase
  - Characterized by progressive penile deformity and painful erection
- Stable phase
  - Chronic phase
  - Characterized by the lack of progression of penile deformity and pain

Clinical features
- Penile pain
- Penile nodules/indurations on the affected side of the penis
- Erectile dysfunction due to abnormal curvature of the penis
- Possibly associated with psychological conditions (eg, anxiety, depression)

Differential diagnosis
- Penile fracture (penile injury → rupture of corpora cavernosa → penile curvature)
- Chordee without hypospadias

Treatment
- Active phase:
  - oral NSAIDs or oral pentoxifylline for 3 months
  - No symptomatic improvements: intralesional collagenase injections
  - Symptomatic improvement: observation or continuation of oral pentoxifylline for another 6 months
- Stable phase:
  - Observation: patients with a mild penile curvature (<30°) and no erectile dysfunction
  - Intralesional collagenase injections: patients with penile curvature (>30°) and/or erectile dysfunction
  - Surgical repair: patients unresponsive to treatment, with severe penile deformity, and/or with extensive calcifications

questionText:
65 years old male patient presented with recurrent episodes of painless hematuria. What is your further management?
a. cystoscopy
b. urine RME
c. USG
d. IVU
explanation:
HEMATURIA
Gross hematuria is visibly bloody urine, whereas microscopic hematuria is defined as three or more red blood cells per high-power field on microscopic evaluation of urinary sediment from two of three properly collected urinalysis (UA)

A. Evaluation consists of laboratory, radiologic, and urine studies.
1. Urinalysis (macro- and microscopic), urine culture, and urine cytology should be obtained from a freshly voided specimen.
2. A complete blood count, coagulation panel, and serum creatinine should be obtained.
3. Radiographic imaging should be obtained to evaluate both the renal parenchyma and the renal collecting system. Cross-sectional imaging provides the most information with respect to total abdominal and pelvic anatomy. Computed tomography (CT) urogram is the preferred imaging modality; however, magnetic resonance (MR) urogram and renal ultrasound with retrograde pyelograms are adequate in appropriately selected patients (i.e., intravenous (IV) dye allergy, pregnancy).
4. Cystoscopy is the gold standard for evaluating the lower urinary tract.
5. If the etiology of the hematuria remains unclear, the patient should have a repeat UA, urine cytology, and blood pressure measurement at 6, 12, 24, and 36 months
Ref: WASHINGTON manual of surgery

Most constant and persistent feature of CA bladder is:
a. Increased frequency
b. Hematuria
c. Recurrent UTI
d. Pain abdomen
explanation:
Carcinoma Urinary Bladder
- More common in whites, higher socio-economic status and in males, in 6th and 7th decade
- 75% are localized to bladder and 25% have spread to regional nodes or distant sites at the time of presentation
- Most tumors develop at trigone and adjacent posterolateral wall with ureteral involvement
- Tumors tend to be multifocal in bladder

Pathology
- MC type grossly is papillary and histologically, TCC
- Precursor lesions of invasive urothelial cancer:
  - Non-invasive papillary tumor (Kyo ulcer) - painless, profuse paroxysmal hematuria
  - Carcinoma in situ (Malignant cystitis)
- Carcinoma in situ (Malignant cystitis)
  - Typically presents as irritative lower symptoms
  - Common in high grade tumors
  - Urinary cytology is IOC
  - Urine cytology is positive in 80-90% cases because poor cohesiveness of cells
  - Associated with increased chances of recurrence, poor prognosis
  - Treatment: Two cycles of BCG, radical cystectomy cases recurrence

Clinical Features
- MC symptom: Painless hematuria (85% cases)
- Hematuria is gross or microscopic, intermittent than constant
- Vesical irritability: frequency, urgency and dysuria
- Bone pain and abdominal pain in advanced disease
- MC site of lymphatic metastases: Pelvic lymph (obturator is MC)
- MC site of hematogenous spread: liver > lung

Diagnosis
- Cystoscopy
  - Diagnosis and initial staging is made by cystoscopy and transurethral resection (TUR)
- Urinary Cytology:
  - Cytologic examination of exfoliated cells in urine in detecting cancer in symptomatic patients and assessing response to treatment
  - Most useful for early diagnosis of recurrence
- Exfoliated Markers for detection of bladder cancer
  - Newer urinary tumor markers like BTA test, nuclear matrix protein (NMP22) can detect specific proteins in urine (BTA/NMP22)
  - Hyaluronidase, Lewis-X antigen on exfoliated urothelial cells
  - Determination of telomerase activity in exfoliated cells
  - Have been used to detect new index tumors and recurrent tumors
  - Expected to play important role in near future
- CT and MRI: used for staging

Management
- Cystoscopy and TUR or biopsy; further management based on stage, grade, size, multiplicity and recurrence pattern

Prognosis
- There is strong correlation between tumor grade and stage and tumor recurrence, progression and survival
- In patients with organ confined disease, presence of lymph node metastases appears to be the most important prognostic factor
- Presence of lymphovascular invasion is associated with poor prognosis

☞ A lucid interval is a temporary improvement in a patient's consciousness after a traumatic brain injury, after which the condition deteriorates. Lucid interval is seen in epidural hemorrhage.
☞ Extradural haematoma is a neurosurgical emer-gency. It results from rupture of an artery, vein or venous sinus, in association with a skull fracture. Typically, it is damage to the middle meningeal artery under the thin temporal bone. A low energy injury mechanism, perhaps with brief loss of con-sciousness, is sufficient to start the extradural bleeding. The patient may then present in the subsequent lucid interval with headache, but without any neurological deficit.

☞ Extradural Hematoma
- EDH is a neurosurgical emergecny
- Nearly alwasy associated with a skull fracture
- More common in young male patients
- Associated with tearing of meningeal artery
- Hematoma accumulates in the space between bone and dura.
- MC slite: Temporal (pterion is th inest part of skull and overlies middle meningeal artery)
- Not always arterial; disruption of a major dural vein surprisingly smal a fall from standing or a simple blow to the head.
- Classical presentation: Intial injury followed by a lucid interval (occuring in <1/3rd of cases)
- Early recognition and treatment can result in recovery from secondary brain injury.
- EDH on CT scan: Lentiform (lens shaped or biconvex hyperdense lesion between the skull and brain
- Treatment of EDH: Immediate surgical evacuation via a craniotomy.
- Overall mortality for all cases of EDH is about 18% and for isolated EDH it is about 2%

questionText: On plain CT scan of head, appearance of subdural hematoma of 2 days is: [Shrawan 2076]
explanation:
☞ CT scan appearance of SDH
☞ The appearance of SDHs on CT varies with clot age and organization.
☞ Hyperacute: In most instances, patients are not imaged in the hyperacute phase (first hour or so), but on occasion when this is performed they appear relatively isodense (Grey) to the adjacent cortex, with a swirled appearance due to a mixture of the clot, serum and ongoing unclotted blood.
☞ Acute: The classic appearance of an acute subdural hematoma is a crescent-shaped homogeneously hyperdense (white) extra-axial collection that spreads diffusely over the affected hemisphere. As the clot starts to retract the density increases typically to >50-60 HU and is thus hyperdense relative to the cortex.
☞ Subacute: As the clot ages and protein degradation occurs, the density starts to drop. At some point between 3 and 21 days (typically 10-14 days), the density will drop to ~ 35-40 HU and become isodense to the adjacent cortex, making identification potentially tricky, especially if subdural collections are bilateral.
☞ Chronic: By definition, it is at least 3 weeks old. The subdural collection becomes hypodense (black) and can reach ~0 HU and be isodense to CSF, and mimic a subdural hygroma. A crescentic shape may change to a biconvex one.
☞ Acute on chronic: Acute on chronic subdural hematomas refers to a second episode of acute hemorrhage into a pre-existing chronic subdural hematoma. It typically appears as a hypodense collection with a hematocrit level (located posteriorly).
Ref:https://radiopaedia.org/articles/subdural-haemorrhage

questionText: Which of the following is not true about intussusception? [Shrawan 2076]
options: Most commonly affects the children of age group 5 months to 10 months

Child is normal in between episodes
Managed non-operatively with hydrostatic reduction by enema using contrast or air
explanation:
Intussusception
This occurs when one portion of the gut invaginates into an immediately adjacent segment; almost invariably, it is the proximal into the distal.
The condition is encountered most commonly in children, with a peak incidence between 5 and 10 months of age.
About 90% of cases are idiopathic but an associated upper respiratory tract infection or gastroenteritis may precede the condition.
It is believed that hyperplasia of Peyer's patches in the terminal ileum may be the initiating event.
Weaning, loss of passively acquired maternal immunity and common viral pathogens have all been implicated in the pathogenesis of intussusception in infancy.
Intussusception may be anatomically defined according to the site and extent of invagination. In most children, the intussusception is ileocolic. In adults, colocolic intussusception is more common.

Imaging in intussusception
A plain abdominal field: small or large bowel obstruction with an absent caecal gas shadow in ileocolic cases.
A barium enema: the claw sign.
An abdominal ultrasound scan has a high diagnostic sensitivity in children, demonstrating the typical doughnut appearance of concentric rings in transverse section.
CT scanning is currently considered the most sensitive radiological method to confirm intussusception, with a reported diagnostic accuracy of 58-100%. The characteristic features of CT scan include a 'target' or 'sausage' sign.

Treatment of intussusception
In the infant with ileocolic intussusception, non-operative resuscitation with intravenous fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics and nasogastric drainage, reduction can be attempted using an air or barium enema.
Non-operative reduction is contraindicated if there are signs of peritonitis or perforation, there is a known pathological lead point or in the presence of profound shock.
In experienced units, more than 70% of intussusceptions can be reduced non-operatively.
Surgery is required when radiological reduction has failed or is contraindicated.
Ref: Bailey and Love's Short Practice Of Surgery 27th Chapter Intestinal obstruction

questionText: 2 years male child presented with abdominal pain, vomiting and not passing stool for 1 day. Clinical features of intussusception
The classical presentation of intussusception is episodes of screaming and drawing up of the legs in previously well male infant.
The attacks last for a few minutes and recur repeatedly. During attacks the child appears pale between episodes may be listless.
Vomiting may or may not occur at the outset but becomes conspicuous and bile-stained with time.
Initially, the passage of stool may be normal, whereas later, blood and mucus are evacuated - the 'red currant jelly' stool.
Classically, the abdomen is not initially distended, and that hardens on palpation may be discerned but this is present in only 60% of cases.
There may be an associated feeling of emptiness in right iliac fossa (the sign of Dance).
On rectal examination, blood-stained mucus may be found on the finger.
Unrelieved, progressive dehydration and abdominal distension from small bowel obstruction will be followed by peritonitis secondary to gangrene.
Ref: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27th edition Page no. 1287

questionText: Meckel's diverticulum found in hernia sac is called [Mangsir 2073]
explanation:
Meckel's diverticulum
• A Meckel's diverticulum is a persistent remnant of the vitellointestinal duct and is present in about 2% of the population. It is found on the anti-mesenteric side of the ileum, commonly approximately 60 cm from the ileocaecal valve and is classically 5 cm long. A Meckel's diverticulum is a congenital diverticulum. It contains all three coats of the bowel wall and has its own blood supply. It may be vulnerable to obstruction and inflammation in the same way as the appendix; indeed, when a normal appendix is found at surgery for suspected appendicitis, a Meckel's diverticulum should be looked for by examining the terminal bowel, particularly if free fluid or pus is found. In approximately 20% of cases, the mucosa of a Meckel's diverticulum contains heterotopic epithelium of gastric, colonic or pancreatic type. The presence of heterotopic mucosa may predispose to the development of complications. The vast majority of Meckel's diverticula are asymptomatic and Meckel's diverticulum is notoriously difficult to see with contrast radiology. Meckel's diverticulum may, however, present clinically in the following ways:
  - Haemorrhage. If gastric mucosa is present, peptic ulceration can occur and present as painless dark red rectal bleeding or melaena. If the stomach, duodenum and colon are excluded as a source of bleeding by endoscopy, radioisotope scanning with technetium-99m may demonstrate a Meckel's diverticulum.
  - Diverticulitis. Meckel's diverticulitis presents like appendicitis, although if perforation occurs the presentation may resemble a perforated duodenal ulcer.
  - Intussusception. A Meckel's diverticulum can be the lead point for ileoileal or ileocolic intussusception.
  - Chronic ulceration. Pain is felt around the umbilicus, as the site of the diverticulum is midgut in origin.
  - Intestinal obstruction. A band between the apex of the diverticulum and the umbilicus (also part of the Vitellointestinal duct) may cause obstruction directly, or by predisposing to the development of a volvulus around it.
  - Perforation.
When found in the course of abdominal surgery, a Meckel's diverticulum can safely be left alone, provided it has a wide mouth and is not thickened. When there is doubt, it can be resected. The finding of a Meckel's diverticulum in an inguinal or femoral hernia has been described as 'Littre's hernia'.

questionText: A middle aged man with history of recurrent abdominal pain develops sudden onset fever, severe pain abdomen, nausea and vomiting and passage of reddish stool. What is the diagnosis? [Ashoj-II 2080]
explanation:
Meckel diverticulum is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract and is caused by an incomplete obliteration of the omphalomesenteric duct.
It is generally about 2 inches long and located 2 feet proximal to the ileocecal valve.
It is seen in 2% of the general population and is more common in males.
The mucosal lining of the diverticulum may be either native ileal mucosa or heterotopic mucosa (most commonly gastric).
It is often asymptomatic and detected incidentally on imaging or abdominal surgery.
The characteristic presentation of symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding (hematochezia) in children < 2 years. Patients may also present with acute intestinal obstruction (intussusception or volvulus), diverticulitis, and, rarely, peritonitis due to perforation of a Meckel diverticulum
A Meckel diverticulum should be suspected when the work-up of a patient with lower gastrointestinal bleed or acute abdomen reveals no abnormalities.
Sensitive and specific diagnostic tests for Meckel diverticulum include Meckel scan (99m technetium scintigraphy), CT angiography, and diagnostic laparoscopy.
All symptomatic/complicated cases must be surgically resected.
An asymptomatic Meckel diverticulum detected incidentally during abdominal surgery in a child should be resected. In adults < 50 years, only an incidentally detected Meckel diverticulum with risk factors for complications (e.g., a long, broad-based diverticulum) should be resected.
An asymptomatic Meckel diverticulum incidentally detected on imaging does not require treatment.

questionText: Which of the following congenital abnormalities is not correctly defined?
options: Omphalocele represents a defect in the abdominal wall lateral to the umbilical cord.

An umbilical polyp is a small excrescence of omphalomesenteric duct mucosa that is retained in the umbilicus.
Meckel's diverticulum results when the intestinal end of the omphalomesenteric duct persists and represents a true diverticulum.
explanation: Omphalocele may be seen in newborns and represents a defect in the closure of the umbilical ring. The herniated viscera are usually covered with sac. Gastroschisis, a defect of the abdominal wall lateral to the umbilical cord, is caused by failure of closure of the body wall. The intestines protrude through the defect and no sac is present to cover the herniated intestine. In the fetus, the omphalomesenteric duct may present as abnormalities related to the abdominal wall when the duct fails to obliterate. Meckel's diverticulum is the result of the failure of obliteration of the intestinal end of the omphalomesenteric duct. This is a true diverticulum with all layers of the intestinal wall represented. An umbilical polyp is a small excrescence of omphalomesenteric duct mucosa retained in the umbilicus. Such polyps resemble umbilical granulomas except that they do not disappear after silver nitrate cauterization. Appropriate treatment is excision of the mucosal remnant.

questionText: In a skin graft transfer, the word 'take' of graft refers to:
options: Dense attachment of graft to the surrounding tissue
explanation: Graft are tissues that are transferred without their blood supply which therefore have to vascularize once they are in a new site. If the local conditions are favorable, the skin graft obtain a new blood supply from the recipient wound or defect. This process is known as 'take' of graft.

questionText: The earliest manifestation of increased intracranial pressure following head injury is:
explanation: The earliest sign of increased intracranial pressure is alteration of mental status.

questionText: The following statements regarding finasteride are true except:
options: It is used in the medical treatment of benign Prostatic hypertrophy (BPH)
Impotence is well documented after its use
It blocks the conversion of dihydrotestosterone to testosterone
explanation: Finasteride blocks the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone.

questionText: Which of the following catheter materials is most suited for long-term use?
explanation: Silicone catheters can be used for upto 12 weeks.

questionText: All of the following are true for patients of ulcerative colitis associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), except:
options: PSC reverts after a total colectomy
explanation: Colectomy does not alter the course of PSC.

questionText: A new born presented with bloated abdomen shortly after birth with passing of less meconium. A full thickness biopsy of the rectum was carried out. Which one of the following rectal biopsy findings is most likely to be present?
explanation: The history is suggestive of congenital aganglionic megacolon (Hirschsprung's disease). The ganglion cells in the intestinal wall are absent. It occurs due to arrest in migration of neural crest cells.

questionText: Rita, a 45-year-old lady is explored for a perforated duodenal ulcer 6 hours after onset of symptoms. She has a history of chronic peptic ulcer disease treated medically with minimal symptoms. The procedure of choice is:
explanation: The perforated duodenal ulcer is treated with omental patch (Graham's omental patch).

questionText: Which of the following statements is true regarding testicular tumors?
options: Are embryonal cell carcinomas in 95% of cases
Teratomas are more common than seminoma
Usually present after 50 years of age
explanation: 15% of familial and 5% of sporadic cases of testicular tumor are bilateral.

questionText: The most helpful diagnostic radiographic procedure in small bowel obstruction is:
options: Supine and erect x-rays of the abdomen
explanation: The best radiological test is erect and supine abdomen x-ray. Erect x-ray shows the multiple air-fluid level and supine x-ray shows the level of obstruction.

questionText: Which one of the following statements is incorrect regarding stones in the common bile duct?
options: Are suggested by a bile duct diameter > 6 mm in ultrasound
ERCP, sphincterotomy and balloon clearance is now the standard treatment
When removed by exploration of the common bile ducts the T-tube can be removed after 2 days
explanation: T tubes are kept in the bile duct for 7-10 (commonly 10-14) days. It allows track to mature and helps prevent bile leak and biliary peritonitis.

questionText: A 45-year-old man with a history of previous right hemicolectomy for colon cancer presents with colicky abdominal pain which has become constant over the last few hours. He has marked abdominal distension and has had only minimal vomiting of a feculent material. His abdomen is diffusely tender. Abdominal x-ray shows multiple air fluid levels with dilatation of some loops to greater than 3 cm in diameter. The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation: Distinguishing the various types of bowel obstruction can be difficult based on history, physical findings, and radiographic studies. The patient describes an intermittent to constant pain with low volume feculent vomiting. Distension is marked and progressive, and tenderness is diffuse. This scenario most likely fits with distal small bowel obstruction. The feculent vomiting suggests a more distal rather than proximal open loop small bowel obstruction. The lack of severe pain and signs of peritoneal irritation suggests that a closed-loop obstruction is unlikely. A colon obstruction with an incompetent ileocecal valve would be another alternative to consider if gas in the colon had been seen on x-ray.

questionText: A 32-year-old-man with a week's history of fever presently has right lower quadrant abdominal pain and tenderness and bloody diarrhea. The most probable diagnosis is:
explanation: Typhoid ileitis presents with symptoms of fever for about a week or two, headache, pain in abdomen RLQ, and diarrhea.

questionText: Referred pain from all of the following conditions may be felt along the inner side of right thigh, except:
explanation: The pain in the inner side of the thigh is may be referred from appendicitis, inflamed ovaries and ureteric stone.

questionText: In which of the following types of breast carcinoma, would you consider biopsy of opposite breast?
explanation: Lobular carcinoma has higher incidence of laterality compared to other carcinomas.

questionText: Which one of the following statements is incorrect in regard to stones in the gallbladder?
options: Pigment stones are due to increased excretion of conjugated bilirubin
Are considered a risk factor for the development of gallbladder carcinoma
A mucocele of the gallbladder is caused by a stone impacted in Hartman's pouch
explanation: Mucocele of gallbladder is caused by stone impaction in the neck of gall bladder or in the cystic duct.

questionText: One of the following is not correct in papillary carcinoma of thyroid:
options: Can be reliably diagnosed using fine needle aspiration cytology
Typically spreads to the cervical lymph nodes
Requires a total thyroidectomy for large tumours
explanation: Papillary carcinoma is usually multifocal. Lymphatic spread occurs to cervical lymph nodes (Hematogenous spread occurs in case of follicular carcinoma).

questionText: A 26-year old woman in her first trimester of pregnancy presents with a 2-day history of right lower quadrant pain and fever. Physical examination reveals a tender, palpable, right lower quadrant mass. There is no evidence of peritonitis or systemic sepsis. Laboratory evaluation is remarkable for mild leukocytosis, and abdominal ultrasound demonstrates an inflammatory mass but no evidence of abscess. As the surgeon on call, your recommendation would be:
options: Intravenous hydration, antibiotic prophylaxis, and urgent appendectomy
Intravenous hydration, antibiotics, bowel rest, and interval appendectomy in 4 to 6 weeks
Intravenous hydration, antibiotics, and appendectomy if no improvement in 12 to 24 hours
Emergent obstetrical consultation for evaluation and treatment of possible ectopic pregnancy
explanation: The patient presented has a perforated appendix with a phlegmon, but no abscess. One must routinely provide resuscitation and broad spectrum antibiotic coverage in this circumstance. As she is not systemically toxic, it would be rational in a non-pregnant patient to treat this patient non-operatively initially and follow this with interval appendectomy. However, in this circumstance, the risk of preterm labor associated with anesthesia and pelvic inflammation increases with more advanced gestation, so the best decision is to proceed with intravenous hydration, broad spectrum antibiotic coverage and urgent appendectomy.

questionText: Which of the following is a degloving injury?
explanation: Degloving injury is a type of avulsion injury in which an extensive section of skin is completely torn off the underlying tissue, severing its blood supply.

questionText: In which of the following conditions acquired (secondary) megacolon is seen?
options: Complete absence of parasympathetic ganglion cells
explanation: Absence of ganglion cells result in congenital megacolon. Fissure in ano causes anal sphincter spasm, but does not result in megacolon. Rectal malignancies cause obstruction leading to development of megacolon.

questionText: A 34 year-old female patient presented with dysphagia to both liquids and solids and regurgitation for months. The dysphagia was progressive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Esophageal dysphagia flowchart:

[ Esophageal dysphagia ]
  ↓
  ├─ [ Solids and liquids (Neuromuscular) ]
  │     ↓
  │     ├─ [ Progressive ] → Scleroderma / Achalasia
  │     └─ [ Intermittent ] → Diffuse esophageal spasm
  │
  └─ [ Solids only (Mechanical obstruction) ]
        ↓
        ├─ [ Intermittent ] → Lower esophageal ring
        └─ [ Progressive ] → Cancer / Peptic stricture

questionText: Saint triad consists of all, except:
explanation: Saint's triad includes hiatus hernia, diverticulosis and gall stone.

questionText: Gasless abdomen in X-ray is a sign of:
explanation:
Important radiological appearance:
Acute pancreatic: Renal halo sign, Gasless abdomen, Ground glass appearance, colon cut off sign, sentinel loop.
Chronic pancreatic: Chain of lakes appearance, string of pearl appearance, beaded appearance.
CA pancreas: Double contour of medial border of duodenal 'C' loop, double duct sign, scrambled egg appearance, inverted/reverse 3 sign

questionText: Pringle maneuver is digital compression of:
explanation: The operative management of liver injuries can be summarized as 'the four Ps': Push, Pringle, Plug & Pack. At laparotomy, the liver is reconstituted as best as possible in its normal position and bleeding is controlled by direct compression (push). The inflow from the portal triad is controlled by a Pringle's maneuver, with direct compression of the portal triad, either digitally or using a soft clamp. This has the effect of reducing arterial and portal venous inflow into the liver, although it does not control the backflow from the inferior vena cava and hepatic veins. Any holes due to penetrating injury can be plugged directly and, after controlling any bleeding, the liver can then be packed (as a part of Damage control surgery).

questionText: A patient is receiving a blood transfusion after reoperative laparotomy for small bowel obstruction. The nurse notes that blood has clotted in the tube of IV set. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Transfusion of the blood with the same iv set containing ringer lactate causes clotting of the blood because of presence of calcium in the ringer lactate solution.

questionText: Early postoperative complication of ileostomy:
explanation: Postoperative complications that occur with sufficient frequency in ileostomy are: Nipple valve slippage, pouchitis, intestinal obstruction and fistula. Late complications of ileostomy are Obstruction, Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia, Stoma problems, Valve malfunction and Phantom rectum.

questionText: A 45 years old female complains of progressive lower limb weakness, spasticity and urinary hesitancy. MRI shows intradural enhancing mass lesion. Most likely diagnosis is
explanation: Progressive spastic weakness in legs, urinary incontinence, seizures and intradural enhancing mass lesions are suggestive of meningioma.

questionText: A 50 years old male presented with history of hematemesis of around 500 ml of blood and on examination shows BP - 90/60 mmHg, PR - 110 bpm and splenomegaly 5 cm below lower costal margin. Most probable diagnosis is
explanation: The features suggestive of portal hypertension are ascites, esophageal varices and hematemesis, pain abdomen, splenomegaly, jaundice (due to hepatorenal syndrome), features of shock.

questionText: This form of shock has a low blood pressure, low urine output but has an elevated central venous pressure:
explanation:
Table: Cardiovascular and metabolic characteristics of shock

| Parameter | Hypovolaemia | Cardiogenic | Obstructive | Distributive |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cardiac output | Low | Low | Low | High |
| Vascular resistance | High | High | High | Low |
| Venous pressure | Low | High | High | Low |
| Mixed venous saturation | Low | Low | Low | High |
| Base deficit | High | High | High | High |

questionText: What type of shock is caused by the interference of the balance of vasodilator and vasoconstrictor influences to arterioles and venules?
explanation: Neurogenic shock is due to disruption of the autonomic pathways within the spinal cord signified by fall in BP and slowed heart rate.

questionText: An 80-year-old man who has been bedridden for many years following a stroke presents with acute onset of abdominal distention, obstipation, and colicky abdominal pain. Abdominal x-rays reveal dilated loops of small bowel and a dilated sigmoid colon resembling a bent inner tube. Examination reveals distention with mild direct tenderness but no rigidity or rebound tenderness. Initial management should consist of:
options: Laparotomy with resection of descending colon and descending colostomy.
Multiple cleansing enemas to remove impacted feces.
Rigid sigmoidoscopy and decompression of the sigmoid colon.
explanation: This patient appears to have presented with the classic signs and symptoms of acute sigmoid volvulus. The majority of patients with colonic volvulus are elderly men with underlying neurologic dysfunction. They are commonly referred from a chronic care facility. The patient's condition should be assessed immediately. In the absence of peritonitis the preferred initial management consists of urgent endoscopic detorsion of the volvulus. In most patients this can be easily accomplished with a rigid 25-cm sigmoidoscope or a flexible fiberoptic colonoscope. Often detorsion of the sigmoid colon results in a dramatic expulsion of gas and feces. A rectal tube should be introduced into the sigmoid and then taped to the thigh or buttock and left in place to prevent immediate recurrence of the volvulus.

questionText: Barrett's esophagus is diagnosed by the feature of:
explanation: Barrett's esophagus refers to an abnormal change (metaplasia) in the lower portion of esophagus where there is replacement of the normal stratified squamous epithelium by the simple columnar epithelium (which are usually found in lower GIT).

questionText: A patient was brought to the hospital with a history of RTA eight hours back. A few drops of blood is noted at the external urethral meatus. He has not passed urine and his bladder is palpable per abdomen. The probable diagnosis is
options: Urethral injury with extravasation of urine in the retroperitoneum
explanation: The features of urethral injury are: Blood in external meatus, failure or difficulty in passing urine, Extravasation of urine to scrotum, perineum and abdominal wall, Shock with pallor, tachycardia, and hypotension. Features of associated injuries like head injury, thorax and or abdominal organs are present. On P/R examination, prostate may be felt high or may not be palpable at all. Signifies floating prostate.

questionText: In an open injury, during toileting and debridement, muscle viability is detected by all except:
options: Punctate bleeding spots on cut edge
explanation: Here option 'a' is suitable answer. Viability of muscle is assessed by four characters: Color (Normally beefy red), Consistency (Normally firm), Cut (Normally bleeds profusely) and Contractility (Contracts in response to forceps pinch). Dead muscle has purplish color, mushy consistency, failure to contract when stimulated and failure to bleed when cut (except for some arterioles in necrotic muscle which can bleed).

questionText: Which hernia is least likely to strangulate?
explanation: Femoral hernia is most likely to strangulate.

questionText: Hernia with hydrocele is called as:
explanation:
Berger's hernia: hernia in pouch of Douglas
Gibbon's hernia: hernia with hydrocele
Cooper's hernia (bilocular hernia): a femoral hernia with two sacs, the first being in the femoral canal and the second passing through a defect in the superficial fascia and appearing immediately beneath skin.

questionText: External hemorrhoids below the dentate line are:
options: Skin tag is not seen in these cases
explanation: External hemorrhoids below the dentate line are painful because there is somatic nerve supply by inferior rectal nerves.

questionText: A 60 year old smoker came with the history of painless gross hematuria for one day. The investigation of choice would be:
explanation: Painless gross hematuria in an elderly smoker indicates the diagnosis of urinary tract malignancy.

questionText: True about Branchial cyst is:
options: Cysts are more common than sinuses
explanation: Branchial cyst arises due to failure of the obliteration of the second branchial cleft.

questionText: Carcinoembryonic antigens (CEA) is increased in all except:
explanation: CEA is increased in adenocarcinoma of colon, pancreas, breast, ovary and lungs.

questionText: Severity of acute pancreatitis correlate with which of all of the following except:
explanation: Amylase levels can be used to diagnose acute pancreatitis. But there is no correlation between amylase levels and severity of acute pancreatitis.

questionText: Stone which is resistant to lithotripsy
explanation: Cysteine stone is the hardest renal stone. So, it is not suitable for lithotripsy.

questionText: A patient comes with hematemesis and melena. On the upper GI endoscopy there was no significant lesion. 2 days later the patient rebleeds. Next line of investigation is:
explanation: In case of rebleed, laparotomy should be done.

questionText: 30 year old female presented with unilateral breast cancer associated with axillary lymph node enlargement. Modified radical mastectomy was done, further treatment plan will be:
options: Adriamycin based chemotherapy followed by tamoxifen depending on estrogen/progesterone receptor status
explanation: In cases of breast cancer with lymph node involvement, surgery is followed by chemotherapy based on receptor status.

questionText: All of the following are associated with raised serum amylase, except:
explanation: Serum amylase is raised in cases of pancreatitis, perforated peptic ulcer, salivary gland disease, intestinal obstruction, azathioprine therapy, cholecystitis, DKA.

questionText: Most common complication after ERCP is:
explanation: The main complication of ERCP is pancreatitis (3-5%). Other complications are intestinal perforation, bleeding, allergy to contrast medium, bile duct infection.

questionText: All are true regarding hernia except:
options: Femoral hernia is lateral to and below the pubic tubercle
Indirect hernia is medial to inferior epigastric blood vessel
Contents of the sac are anterolateral to the cord
Ovary and fallopian tubes may prolapse into inguinal canal as hernia
explanation: Indirect inguinal hernia lies lateral to inferior epigastric artery and direct inguinal hernia lies medial to inferior epigastric hernia.

questionText: A 20 years old girl presents with 9 month history of neck swelling with thyrotoxic symptoms. On investigation increased T4 and decreased TSH with palpable 2 cm nodule was found. Next investigation will be:
explanation: In cases of thyroid nodule with thyrotoxic symptoms, thyroid scan is indicated.

questionText: A 30 years old male receive blunt abdomen trauma. The incision is best done through:
options: Depends on the severity of hemorrhage
explanation: Exploratory laparotomy is the method of abdominal exploration, a diagnostic tool that allows surgeon to examine the abdominal organs. Midline incision gives you the better exposure of abdominal organs and makes it easy for you to identify and rectify the problem easily.

questionText: The following is a marker of Paget's disease of breast
explanation: CEA- Carcinoembryonic Antigen is the tumor marker in colorectal carcinoma, breast carcinoma (paget's disease of breast as well), cervical cancer, lung cancer and ovarian cancer.

questionText: Which of the following advises is not given to a 38 years old women with recurrent renal stones?
explanation: Calcium intake is not restricted unless calcium levels in serum are very high. Instead reduced calcium intake leads to decreased free calcium in intestines that leads to increased absorption of oxalate. Increased oxalate leads to increased tendency to form renal stones.

questionText: Term for thrombophlebitis of superficial breast veins is:
explanation: Mondor's disease of breast is the thrombophlebitis of the superficial veins of breast.

questionText: Which fruit juice helps in preventing UTI?
explanation:
Advantages of cranberry juice:
* Urine acidification (with cranberry juice or vitamin C) inhibits some bacteria.
* It reduces bacteriuria and pyuria.
* Extract of cranberry juice inhibits the adherence of E. coli to cells lining the bladder.

questionText: HER-2 is associated with
explanation: HER-2/neu is a growth factor receptor protein found in around 20% of all breast cancers. Hence, breast tumors are also stained for c-erbB2 (also known as HER-2/neu), as patients who are positive can be treated with the monoclonal antibody trastuzumab (Herceptin), either in the adjuvant or relapse setting.

questionText: Most common cause of green discharge from the nipple is:
explanation: Greenish discharge from the nipple is seen in duct ectasia.

questionText: On PR examination of a male, which cannot be felt?
explanation: During digital rectal examination, structures felt are anorectal ring, rectal mucosa, prostate, bulb of penis, seminal vesicles.

questionText: Most common breast lesion in adolescent and adults is?
explanation: The most common benign lesion of breast in adolescent and adult female is breast mouse, fibroadenoma.

questionText: Primary test to detect the overproduction of serotonin in carcinoid tumor is:
explanation: The primary test to detect overproduction of serotonin in carcinoid tumor is to check the level of urinary 5-HIAA.

questionText: All of the following form radiolucent stones except:
explanation: Radio-opaque stones are Oxalate, Struvite, cysteine, phosphate & staghorn. Radiolucent are Xanthine, uric acid and urate stones. Allopurinol stones do not exist as such but allopurinol may lead to xanthine stones.

questionText: A high amylase level in pleural fluid suggests a diagnosis of:
explanation: High amylase in pleural fluid may also be seen in pancreatic pleural effusion and esophageal rupture.

questionText: Regarding hirschsprung's disease all are true except:
options: Auerbach's and meissner's plexus are absent.
explanation: Hirschsprung's disease is a form of congenital aganglionic megacolon, where a part or whole of the large intestine or antecedent part of GIT have no ganglionic cells. There is absence of the auerbach's and meissner's plexus. There is enlarged, dilated section of bowel proximally and narrowed, aganglionic portion distally. It usually affects the male.

questionText: Most common content on hernia-en-glissade is:
explanation: Hernia-en-glissade (sliding hernia) mostly contains sigmoid colon.

questionText: Gall stone causes intestinal obstruction when it gets impacted in which part of the intestine commonly:
explanation: Passage of stone through a spontaneous biliary enteric fistula leading to a mechanical bowel obstruction is known as gallstone ileus. Most (75%) of the fistulas develop between the gallbladder and duodenum, occurs in elderly people, and account for 1% of all small bowel obstructions. The most common site of obstruction is the terminal ileum because of its narrow lumen. Abdominal films will demonstrate evidence of an intestinal obstruction with pneumobilia or calcified stone in the gall bladder. Relieving the obstruction by removing the gallstone through proximal enterotomy is the main management of gallstone ileus; the stone is milked proximally and then removed from a healthy portion of bowel.

questionText: Which of the following is most common complication after appendectomy?
explanation: The common complication of appendicitis is wound infection.

questionText: Lymphatic drainage of the female breast is predominantly into the following group of lymph node:
explanation: Lymphatic drainage of the female breast is 75% in axillary lymph node (pectoral, scapular, humoral)-75% and rest in parasternal nodes. Among the axillary lymph nodes main drainage is through pectoral group.

questionText: After influenza infection a lady developed pain over thyroid swelling, diagnosis is
explanation:
De Quervain's subacute granulomatous thyroiditis is due to viral etiology either mumps or coxsackie viruses causing inflammatory response.

Classification of thyroid swellings:
a. Simple goiter (euthyroid): Diffuse hyperplastic (Physiological, Pubertal or Pregnancy)
b. Toxic: Multinodular goiter or Diffuse (Graves' disease and Multinodular toxic adenoma)
c. Neoplastic - Benign or Malignant
d. Inflammatory:
i. Autoimmune: Chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis & Hashimoto's disease
ii. Granulomatous: De Quervain's thyroiditis
iii. Fibrosing: Riedel's thyroiditis
iv. Infective: Acute (bacterial thyroiditis, viral thyroiditis, subacute thyroiditis) or Chronic (tuberculous, syphilitic)
v. Other: Amyloid

questionText: Treatment of chronic pseudopancreatic cyst is
explanation: Chronic pseudopancreatic cyst is treated with cystogastrotomy, cystoduodenostomy, cystojejunostomy, or endoscopic stenting.

questionText: Suture material used to suture intestine is
explanation: Absorbable suture like vicryl are used to suture the intestine in layers.

questionText: Regarding bile duct injuries following Cholecystectomy which of the following statements is false?
options: The incidence following open cholecystectomy which is in the range of 0.2-0.3%
The incidence rate following Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy is three times higher than the rates following open cholecystectomy
Untreated cases may develop secondary biliary cirrhosis
Routine use of open technique of laparoscopic port insertion has resulted in a decline in the incidence of post laparoscopic cholecystectomy bile duct injuries
explanation: The risk of bile duct injury is 0.2% in open cholecystectomy and 0.6% in lap-cholecystectomy. The untreated cases have risk of developing biliary cirrhosis.

questionText: During nutritional assessment of a surgical patient, the status of muscle protein is indicated by which of the following parameter?
explanation: Albumin is not a measure of nutritional status. Although a low serum albumin level (<30 g/L) is an indicator of poor prognosis, hypoalbuminaemia invariably occurs because of alterations in body fluid composition and because of increased capillary permeability related to ongoing sepsis. Anthropometric techniques incorporating measurements of skinfold thicknesses and mid-arm circumference permit estimations of body fat and muscle mass, and these are indirect measures of energy and protein stores. MUAC is here the best measure of muscle mass.

questionText: Solitary hypoechoic lesion of the liver without sepate or debris is most likely to be:
explanation: Solitary hypoechoic lesions with no septations seen in liver during USG are simple cyst.

questionText: All of the following are features of Zollinger Ellison syndrome except:
options: Beta cell tumors of the pancreas
explanation: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is caused by a non-beta islet cell gastrin secreting tumor of the pancreas. Symptoms include: chronic diarrhea, pain abdomen, wheezing, vomiting, nausea, loss of weight, peptic ulcers.

questionText: A 20-year-old man suffers an injury to the posterior urethra. After appropriate initial management and follow-up care of this injury, the most likely late complication is:
explanation: Urethral stricture is common complication of the urethral injury.

questionText: Most common organ damaged in penetrating injury of abdomen is:
explanation:
Here the answer is small intestine > liver.
* Most common organ injured in blunt trauma abdomen is: spleen
* Most common organ injured in air-blast injury is: Tympanic membrane (1st) > lung (2nd)
* Least vulnerable organ to the air-blast wave is: liver
* Most common organ injured in under-water blast injury is: Gastrointestinal tract
* Most common organ injured in solid-blast injury (tank, warship) is: bones

questionText: The narrowest part of the ureter is at the:
explanation: Narrowest part of the ureter is at uretero-vesical junction.

questionText: Bikram Jung Thapa, a 26-yrs-old man, sustains a tangential gunshot wound to the lower abdomen. He is awake and normotensive. He has rebound tenderness on physical examination. Which approach is contraindicated?
options: Type and crossmatch 4 units of packed RBCS
explanation: In case of gun-shot injury, if the patient is stable hemodynamically and there is no feature of viscus injury, then surgery is not indicated.

questionText: In which of the following tumor, alpha fetoprotein is elevated?
explanation: Alpha-feto protein is taken as a tumor marker that is elevated in liver carcinoma.

questionText: A 45 year old male presents with 4x4 cm mobile right solitary thyroid nodule of 5 months duration. The patient is euthyroid. The following statements about his management are true except:
options: Cold nodule on thyroid scan is diagnostic of malignancy
FNAC is the investigation of choice
The patient should undergo hemithyroidectomy if FNAC report is inconclusive
Indirect laryngoscopy should be done in the preoperative period to assess mobility of vocal cords.
explanation: Only 20% cold nodule malignant

questionText: Although more than 400 blood groups have been identified, the ABO blood group system remains the most important in clinical medicine because:
options: It was the blood group system to be discovered.
It has four different blood groups A, B, AB, OH
ABO (H) antigens are present in most body tissues and fluids
ABO (H) antibodies are invariably present in plasma when persons RBC lacks corresponding antigen
explanation: The antibodies against the corresponding antigen not present on the surface of the RBCs are present in plasma

questionText: After a minor head injury a young patient was unable to close his left eye and had drooling of saliva from left angle of mouth. He is suffering from
options: Combined VIIth and IIIrd nerve injury
explanation: Inability to close eyes and drooling of saliva from mouth is suggestive of facial nerve injury.

questionText: Following major injuries, damage control surgery is very beneficial before performing a definitive surgery. A patient with the triad of which of the following are at highest risk for performing a protracted surgery in the physiologically unstable patients?
Which of the following is not a contraindication for extra corporeal Shockwave Lithotripsy (ESWL) for renal calculi?
explanation: Contraindications of ESWL are: bleeding diathesis, pregnancy, ureteric stricture, and cysteine stone.

questionText: Investigation of choice in acute cholecystitis:
explanation: Investigation of choice for acute cholecystitis is USG. Gold standard for diagnosis of acute cholecystitis is HIDA scan

questionText: Water lily appearance in a chest radiograph suggests:
explanation: Water lily sign in chest x-ray is suggestive of hydatid cyst

questionText: Which of the following not true of gas gangrene?
options: It is caused by clostridium perfringens
Clostridium Perfringens is a gram-negative spore-bearing bacillus
Gas gangrene is characterized by severe local pain crepitus and signs of toxemia
High dose penicillin and aggressive debridement of affected tissue is the treatment of established infection
explanation: Clostridium Perfringens are Gram +ve spore-bearing bacillus.

questionText: A 25-year-old man is brought to the ER after sustaining burns during a fire in his apartment. He has blistering and erythema of his face, left upper extremity and chest with frank charring of his right upper extremity. He is agitated, hypotensive and tachycardic. Which one of the following statements concerning this patients' initial wound management is correct?
options: Topical antibiotics should not be used, as they will encourage growth resistant organisms
Early excision of facial and hand burns is especially important
Escharotomy should only be performed if neurologic impairment is imminent
Excision of areas of 3rd degree or deep 2nd degree burns usually take place 3 to 7 days after injury
explanation: In case of burn injury, 2nd and 3rd degree burn wounds are usually excised after 3-7 days.

questionText: A patient undergoes a breast biopsy, which demonstrates breast cancer. Estrogen receptor activity is clinically useful in predicting?
explanation: ER-positive tumors receive endocrine therapies and HER-2 positive cancers are treated with inhibitors of HER-2.

questionText: For re-implantation surgery, the detached digit or limb is best preserved in:
explanation:
a. The amputated part is cleaned with a sterile isotonic solution and wrapped in moist sterile gauze. It should be then sealed in waterproof bag.
b. This bag is now placed in container of ice and sent to the reimplantation centre. Permissible ischemic time is maximum 8 hours for proximal amputation whereas 12 hours for the digits.

questionText: Indication for surgery in a child with umbilical hernia is:
explanation: Surgery is needed in a case of umbilical hernia if it fails to reduce by 3 years of age, signs of intestinal obstruction or size > 2 cm.

questionText: Spermatic cord does not contain:
explanation:
Contents of spermatic cord:
* Remains of process vaginalis
* Ductus deferens
* Artery to ductus deferens, testicular artery and cremasteric artery.
* Pampiniform plexus of veins
* Lymphatics
* Genital branch of genitofemoral nerve
* Sympathetic nerves around the artery to ductus deference.

questionText: Axillary abscess is drained through which wall of axilla?
explanation: An axillary abscess should be incised through the floor of axilla, midway between the anterior and posterior axillary folds and nearer to medial wall in order to avoid injury to main vessels running along the anterior, posterior and lateral walls.

questionText: Patient presents with penetrating injury to the right flank. What is the next step in management of this case?
explanation: In modern trauma centers in the 21st century, better non-invasive technology favors the use of Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) and CT in the evaluation of trauma victims.

questionText: What operation is not advised for morbid obesity?
explanation:
Morbid obesity is a term used when BMI is more than 40 in a person.

Classification of bariatric procedures:
1. Restrictive procedures: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGBP), Laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding (reversible and highly safe bariatric surgical procedure), vertical band gastroplasty

questionText: What is normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure?
explanation:
Central venous pressure
CVP or right atrial pressure (RAP) is monitored using a catheter inserted via either the internal jugular or the subclavian vein, with the distal end sited in the upper right atrium. The CVP may help in assessing the need for intravascular fluid replacement and the rate at which this should be given.
Pulmonary artery catheterization and pulmonary artery 'wedge' pressure
The CVP is usually an adequate guide to the filling pressures of both sides of the heart. However, certain conditions, such as pulmonary hypertension or right ventricular dysfunction, may lead to raised CVP levels even in the presence of hypovolemia. In these circumstances, it may be appropriate to insert a pulmonary artery flotation catheter so that pulmonary artery pressure and pulmonary artery 'wedge' pressure (PAWP), which approximates to left atrial pressure, can be measured.
The mean PAWP normally lies between 6 and 12 mmHg (measured from the mid-axillary line) but in left heart failure it may be grossly elevated, exceeding 30 mmHg. Provided the pulmonary capillary membranes are intact, the optimum PAWP when managing acute circulatory failure in the critically ill patient is generally 12-15 mmHg, because this will ensure good left ventricular filling without risking hydrostatic pulmonary edema. Pulmonary artery catheters also allow measurement of cardiac output and sampling of blood from the pulmonary artery ('mixed venous' samples), permitting continuous monitoring of the mixed venous oxygen saturation (Sv02) by oximetry. Measurement of SvO2 gives an indication of the adequacy of cardiac output (and hence D02) in relation to the body's metabolic requirements. It is especially useful in low cardiac output states.

questionText: Partial thickness graft is:

Partial thickness skin grafts, also known as split skin graft or Thiersch graft includes all epidermis and part of dermis. They are thin and have easy uptake. They contract upto 40% and are not useful for cosmetic surgeries. These grafts are hairless and do not sweat. They are used to cover all sizes of wound, are of limited durability and will contract. They may be used to provide valuable temporary wound closure before better cosmetic secondary correction after rehabilitation.
Full thickness skin graft (Wolfe graft) includes all epidermis and dermis. The uptake is difficult because of thickness. There is very minimal contraction, making it suitable for cosmetic surgeries on face. Used for smaller areas of skin replacement where good elastic skin that will not contract is required (such as fingers, eyelids, facial parts).

questionText: A patient on TPN for 20 days presents with weakness, vertigo and convulsions. Diagnosis is:
explanation:
Refeeding syndrome:
This syndrome is characterised by severe fluid and electrolyte shifts in malnourished patients undergoing refeeding. It is more common with prolonged parenteral nutrition. It results in hypophosphataemia, hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia. These electrolyte disorders can result in altered myocardial function, arrhythmias, deteriorating respiratory function, liver dysfunction, seizures, confusion, coma, tetany and death. Patients at risk include those with alcohol dependency, those suffering severe malnutrition, anorexics and those who have undergone prolonged periods of fasting. Treatment involves matching intakes with requirements and assiduously avoiding overfeeding. Calorie delivery should be increased slowly and vitamins administered regularly. Hypophosphataemia and hypomagnesaemia require treatment

questionText: Albumin for parenteral use is restricted to limited cases only because:
options: C. Does not raise oncotic pressure
explanation: Human albumin solution is available for medical use, usually at concentrations of 5-25%. Albumin is expensive and is derived from human donor blood. In terms of efficacy, mortality and cardiorespiratory function, there is little evidence that albumin solutions are better than plasma substitutes or normal saline for resuscitating patients with traumatic or septic shock or requiring large peroperative volume replacement Transfusion of albumin solutions should probably be restricted to patients with hypoproteinaemic oedema withnephrotic syndrome or with ascites in chronic liver disease. Other uses are difficult to justify in the absence ofscientifically proven benefit.

Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis in infancy:

Clinical features:
1. Projectile vomiting between 2-8 weeks, non-bilous curd milk after feed, therefore baby becomes hungry immediately
2. Dehydration and weight loss
Diagnosis:
1. Test feed: characteristic peristaltic wave (left right) across upper abdomen,
2. Palpation: tumor/olive (right upper quadrant)

Treatment:

questionText: A 12 months old male child suddenly draws up his legs and screams with pain. This is repeated periodically throughout the night interspersed with periods of quiet sleep. When seen after 12 hours the child looks pale, has just vomited and passed thin blood stained stool. There is a mass around umbilicus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Intussusception
One part of bowel telescopes into other
Common in infants and toddlers (4-10 months)
Most common type: ileocolic
Typically characterized by sudden, short duration, crampy abdominal pain.
During the episodes infant cries inconsolably and pulls knees up. Stool may be mixed with blood and mucus: currant jelly stool.
Signs: Sausage shaped abdominal mass, with feeling of emptiness in right iliac fossa (sign of Dance).
USG: Kidney shaped mass in longitudinal view and target sign in transverse view.
Plain X-ray: Features of small intestinal obstruction, Target sign, meniscus view.
Target sign: Soft tissue mass with concentric area of lucency due to mesenteric fat.
Meniscus sign: Crescent of gas within colonic lumen outlines the apex of intussusception.
Barium enema: claw sign, coiled spring sign
Claw sign: Rounded apex of intussusception protrudes into the contrast column.
Coiled spring sign: Edematous mucosal folds of outer limb of intussusception outlined by contrast material.
Treatment: Hydrostatic reduction by contrast medium or air enema is the diagnostic and therapeutic procedure of choice. Failure of this mandates operative intervention.

questionText: Most common site of volvulus:
explanation:
Volvulus can occur in any segment of a bowel attached to a long and floppy mesentery or fixed to retroperitoneum by a narrow base of origin. Most common site of volvulus is sigmoid colon and more commonly occurs anticlockwise.
Contrast enema demonstrates the point of obstruction with the pathognomic 'Bird's beak' or 'bird of prey' or 'ace of spades' sign.
Plain X-ray (diagnostic in 70-80%): (coffee bean sign)—single, grossly distended loop of colon arising from the pelvis and extending towards the diaphragm or Coffee bean sign or Bent-inner tube sign.

questionText: What is the treatment of sigmoid volvulus is with suspicion of impending gangrene?
explanation:
Management of sigmoid volvulus.
A flatus tube or Sigmoidoscope is passed in operation theatre (proper care is taken otherwise it leads to perforation). If it derotates, patient will pass flatus and feces and distension reduces.
If derotation does not occur, laparotomy through midline incision should be done. Dilated sigmoid colon is derotated manually and checked for viability. If viable, it can be fixed to the lateral wall of abdomen or pelvis-sigmoidopexy.
If sigmoid colon is gangrenous, it is resected and proximal cut end is brought out as colostomy and distal end is brought out as mucous fistula, from the rectum (Paul-Mikulicz Operation). Later after 6 weeks, continuity is maintained after proper preparation.
Resection of the gangrenous sigmoid done; proximal cut is brought out as end colostomy; distal end closed—Hartmann's operation. Later in 6-12 weeks colorectal anastomosis is maintained.
Primary resection and anastomosis is not advisable because of the contamination and anastomotic leak.
In young patients, an elective sigmoid colectomy is required. It is reasonable not to offer any further treatment following successful endoscopic decompression in the elderly as there is a high death rate (~80 per cent at two years) from causes other than recurrent volvulus.
A Paul-Mikulicz procedure is useful, particularly if there is suspicion of impending gangrene; an alternative procedure is a sigmoid colectomy and, when anastomosis is considered unwise, a Hartmann's procedure with subsequent reanastomosis can be carried out.

questionText: Postoperative ileus is most pronounced in:
explanation:
Postoperative ileus: The motility of the GI tract is transiently impaired following most abdominal operations or injuries. Return of motility takes time [Small intestine (within 24hrs) > Gastric (48 hrs) > Colonic (3-5) days]
Postoperative small bowel motility returns before colonic and gastric motility. Listening to bowel sounds is not a reliable indicator that ileus has fully resolved.

questionText: Which of the following is not a cardinal feature of intestinal obstruction?
explanation: Absolute constipation (obstipation) is the cardinal feature along with vomiting, colicky abdominal pain and abdominal distention.

questionText: All are true except regarding the radiological findings in intestinal obstruction:
options: Jejunum is characterized by valvulae conniventes
Haustral folds completely pass across the width and regularly placed
Two fluid levels in small intestine is considered normal
explanation:
The jejunum is characterised by its valvulae conniventes, which completely pass across the width of the bowel and are regularly spaced, giving a 'concertina' or ladder effect
Ileum: the distal ileum has been piquantly described by Wangensteen as featureless.
Caecum: a distended caecum is shown by a rounded gas shadow in the right iliac fossa.
Large bowel, except for the caecum, shows haustral folds, which, unlike valvulae conniventes, are spaced irregularly, do not cross the whole diameter of the bowel and do not have indentations placed opposite one another.
Radiological features of obstruction (on plain x-ray)
In adults, two inconstant fluid levels-one at the duodenal cap and the other in the terminal ileum—may be regarded as normal.

questionText: Acute pseudo obstruction of the colon is known as:
explanation:
Ogilvie's syndrome: It is acute colonic pseudo obstruction. It is due to malfunctioning sacral parasympathetic nerves. Splenic flexure is the junction of collapsed and dilated large bowel. Descending colon is atonic causing acute functional obstruction. It may be due to trauma, retroperitoneal irritation, antidepressants, uraemia, diabetes, myxoedema, and hypokalemia.
Prokinetic drugs, colonoscopic decompression, tube caecostomy are the treatment.

questionText: A plain abdominal X-ray in a patient with a sigmoid volvulus will show a distended bowel loop with its apex in:
explanation:
The radiographic findings show a markedly dilated sigmoid colon with the appearance of a bent inner tube with its apex in the right upper quadrant. An air-fluid level may be seen in the dilated loop of colon, and gas is usually absent from the rectum.
CT reveals a characteristic mesenteric whorl. A contrast enema typically demonstrates the point of obstruction with the pathognomic bird's beak deformity revealing the twist that obstructs the sigmoid lumen.

questionText: The treatment of caecal volvulus is:
options: Colonoscopic detorsion, bowel preparation and elective resection
Operative detorsion, right hemicolectomy and ileo-colostomy
explanation: Caecal volvulus is second common site for volvulus (30%) following sigmoid volvulus (65%). It is commonest cause of large intestinal obstruction in pregnancy. Resection and anastomosis is the only treatment

questionText: A suspected case of intestinal obstruction shows pneumobilia. What is your diagnosis?
explanation: Pneumobilia (gas in the biliary tree) is typical finding in case of intestinal obstruction due to gall stone ileus.

questionText: A 10 year-old women is seen with abdominal pain and obstipation. On examination, she is afebrile with slight tachycardia. Her abdomen is distended and tympanic, but there are no peritoneal signs. Abdominal x-ray suggests the presence of sigmoid volvulus. The first step in her management should be:
options: Administration of laxatives and cleansing enemas
explanation: In case of sigmoid volvulus, a flatus tube or sigmoidoscope is passed in operation theatre (proper care is taken otherwise it leads to perforation). If it derotates, patient will pass flatus and faeces and distension reduces. If derotation does not occur, laparotomy is done through midline incision, derotation is done manually, viability is checked and if it is viable, sigmoidopexy is done. If not viable, resection and colostomy is done.

questionText: Distended abdomen in intestinal obstruction is mainly due to:
explanation:
Cause of abdominal distension in intestinal obstruction are
* Gas: Swallowed air is the major source (nitrogen is not well absorbed by intestinal mucosa). Gases produced by bacterial fermentation are also responsible.
* Fluid: Fluid from extracellular space (third space loss) to GI secretion is also enhanced in obstruction.

questionText: The best type of x-ray to locate free abdominal air is:
options: A postero-anterior view of the chest
A flat and upright view of the abdomen
A lateral decubitus x-ray, right side up
explanation: Free gas in abdomen is best diagnosed with an x-ray in lateral decubitus.

questionText: Complete mechanical small bowel obstruction can cause dehydration by:
explanation: The causes of dehydration in a case of obstruction are, vomiting, defective absorption, intramural inflammation leading to intestinal hypoxia

questionText: Characteristic of Crohn's disease
explanation:
Crohn's disease is a chronic transmural inflammatory disease of the GIT, involving any part of the alimentary tract from mouth to anus but most commonly affects the small intestine and colon. Diseased bowel is separated by areas of grossly appearing normal bowel. Perianal disease (Tissue, fistula, stricture or abscess) is common. And manifestation can be most devastating because of their painful nature and their threat to the patient's incontinence. Anal fissure is most common anal problem in Crohn's disease. It may lead into perianal abscess and fistula.
Main features of Crohn's disease
* Ileum—most common site of occurrence—60%
* Rectal sparing is usual and common
* Skip lesion
* Hose-pipe pattern
* Linear ulcers and cobble stone appearance of mucosa
* Transmural involvement

questionText: Which answers is true? In contrast to ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease of the colon:
options: Is not associated with increased risk of colon cancer
Has a lower incidence of perianal fistulas
explanation: Crohn's disease of the colon is a patchy, segmental (rather than continuous), chronic, transmural inflammatory process that penetrates the bowel wall to form fistulas but rarely causes rectal bleeding. In contrast, ulcerative colitis is a mucosal ulcerating process that extends continuously from the rectum to the more proximal colon and frequently bleeds. Both diseases can develop toxic megacolon and both predispose the patient to increased risk of malignancy of the large intestine over the long term.

questionText: Toxic megacolon is seen in:
explanation:
Toxic megacolon is a serious life threatening condition that can occur in patients of ulcerative colitis and infectious colitis such as pseudomembranous colitis.
Toxic megacolon with acute colitis even though rare can occur in Crohn's disease.

questionText: What is the most common extra-intestinal manifestation of Chron's disease of small intestine?
explanation:
Skin lesions are the most common extra-intestinal manifestations unlike in ulcerative colitis where arthritis is more common. Extra-intestinal manifestations of Crohn's disease
* Skin: Erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum—most common
* Eyes: Iritis, uveitis
* Joints: Arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis
* Sclerosing cholangitis
* Nephrotic syndrome
* Pancreatitis
* Amyloidosis
* Blood: Anaemia, thrombocytosis, DVT, arterial thrombosis

questionText: All are true about superior mesenteric artery syndrome, except:
options: Obstruction of the 3rd part of the duodenum
Non-bilious vomiting, upper abdominal fullness and visible peristalsis seen
It is also known as chronic duodenal ileus
explanation:
Chronic Duodenal Ileus (Wilkie's Syndrome)
* It is also called as superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome which is due to obstruction of the 3rd part of the duodenum due to decreased angle between SMA and aorta.
* It can be congenital or due to low insertion of SMA or high insertion of duodenal end or due to traumatic aneurysm of SMA.
* It can be aggravated by plaster casts, lordosis, pancreatic tumor, enlarged lymph node in the 3rd part of duodenum (Cast syndrome).
* Clinical Features are bilious vomiting, upper abdominal fullness, visible peristalsis and dehydration.
* Differential Diagnosis are pyloric stenosis with gastric outlet obstruction and annular pancreas.
* Barium meal is diagnostic, CT scan abdomen is also quite helpful
* Treatment consists of duodenojejunostomy (Gastrojejunostomy—not done).

questionText: Typhoid perforation is diagnosed by:
options: Plain X-ray of abdomen in erect posture
explanation: The pathognomic of hollow viscus perforation is the presence of gas shadow under right dome of diaphragm which is seen in erect X-ray of abdomen, more preferably an erect chest X-Ray.

questionText: Commonest site of tuberculosis of the intestines:
explanation:
Intestinal Tuberculosis
* Mycobacterium tuberculosis is the responsible for all cases of GI tuberculosis.
* Primary intestinal tuberculosis: Ingestion of contaminated food Hyperplastic: lymphoid involvement, thickening of intestinal wall and narrowing of lumen
* Secondary intestinal tuberculosis: Arrives from swallowed Sputum containing tuberculosis bacilli Ulcerative: transverse ulcers.
* MC site is terminal ileum and ileocaecal junction.
* Most common symptoms: abdominal pain, diarrhea is also common.
* Stricture formation occurs in sclerotic variant
* MC complications are intestinal obstruction and malabsorption.
* USG: Club-sandwich appearance.

questionText: Which of the following is true of small bowel carcinoids?
options: It does not cause endocardial fibrosis
It is the most common malignancy of small intestine
explanation:
Carcinoids: neuroendocrine tumor (malignant tumor of enterochromaffin cell origin)
* Location >90% in GI tract (Sites: appendix: 46% > ileum: 28% > Rectum: 17%
* Arise from Kulchitsky cells (argentaffin cells secreting serotonin, histamine, prostaglandins, and kallikrein) at the base of crypts of lieberkuhn in the GI tract.
* Clinical features: Asthmatic attacks, Borborygmi, Cyanosis, Diarrhea, Pulmonary and Tricuspid Stenosis, Flushing attacks induced by alcohol.
* Investigations: Diagnosis by Elevated urinary level of 5-HIAA (hydroxyl indole acetic acid) measured in 24 hours urine sample Octreotide scanning, chromogranin A concentration.
* Treatment:
a. Medical for symptoms of carcinoid syndrome: serotonin antagonists (cyproheptadine) or somatostatin analogue (octreotide); Octeatride cover during surgery to prevent carcinoid crisis & to decrease flushing and diarrhea in metastasis
b. Surgical resection:
Appendiceal carcinoid: < 2cms → appendectomy, > 2cms—right hemicolectomy
Small intestine carcinoid: resect tumor with mesenteric lymph nodes.
* Midgut carcinoid has the best prognosis
* Malignant potential in carcinoid depends upon the location, size, and depth of invasion and growth pattern.
* Appendiceal carcinoid has lowest rate of metastasis <3% while ileum has metastasis in upto 35% cases.

questionText: Most common site of colonic carcinoma:
explanation: Most common sites of carcinoma: Rectum (most common - 38%); sigmoid colon (2nd MC - 21%), followed by: Transverse colon, ascending colon, descending colon, splenic flexure and hepatic flexure in descending order.

questionText: Constricting type of colonic carcinoma is seen in:
explanation: Colonic carcinoma, on the right side of the large intestine tend to be exophytic, that is, tumor grows outwards from one location in the bowel wall (ulcerative and proliferative type). They rarely cause obstruction of feces. Left sided tumors tend to be circumferential, annular and tubular type, and can obstruct the bowel lumen, much like a napkin ring, and results in thinner caliber stools.

questionText: Carcinoma of right colon presents as:
explanation:
