questionText: Ramu is 60 years old male with CA of descending colon presents with acute intestinal obstruction in emergency department. Treatment of choice is:
explanation: Hartman's procedure: Sigmoidectomy with descending colostomy and closure of the rectal stump. It is the treatment of choice in acute obstruction due to cancer of left side of colon.

questionText: First investigation to be done in patient with recurrent fecal occult blood loss:
explanation: Recurrent fecal occult blood loss is a feature of lower GI malignancy. To visualize the lower GI and rule out growth, colonoscopy is the investigation of choice.

questionText: Typhoid perforation is common in ........ of the disease.
explanation: Typhoid: Paralytic ileus is the commonest complication. Intestinal haemorrhage can occur (10%)—as the Peyer's patches interminal ileum enlarged and ulcerated. Perforation usually occurs in 3rd week of the infection. Ulcers are multiple, arranged in parallel and in antimesenteric border of the ileum, one or more ulcers might perforate and many ulcers may show Impending perforation.

questionText: Which of the following is a reason for why small bowel malignancies are less commoneven though It comprises 75% of length and 90% of GI mucosa?
options: Plenty of lymphoid tissue in the wall provides immunity
Most of the nutrients get absorbed here which provides protection
explanation:
Reasons why malignancy is uncommon in the small bowel (even though it comprises 75% of length and 90% of GI mucosa):
Rapid transit time. 30 minute to 2 hours. So exposure of mucosa to toxins and metabolites is less.
Alkaline mucus rich luminal content is protective
Cells of small bowel produce the enzyme benzopyrene hydroxylase which detoxifies the carcinogen-benzopyrene.
High levels luminal IgA provides immunity.
Plenty of lymphoid tissue in the wall provides immunity.
Healthy small bowel has got less bacterial load and so their toxic metabolites (as compared to colon).

questionText: The most common site of colonic diverticula is:
explanation:
Most common type of diverticular (abnormal sac or pouch protruding from the wall of a hallow organ) are the acquired ones which are false diverticular or pseudo diverticular lacking a portion of normal bowel wall.
* Diverticular disease can present with painless rectal bleeding as bright red blood per rectum. It is the most common cause of acute lower GI bleeding.
* Diverticular disease can affect whole colon except rectum, common in elderly causes include ageing and refined western diet.
Most common site: sigmoid colon
The clinical features of diverticulitis closely mimic that of acute appendicitis, however the pain is localized to left iliac fossa so called sometimes as left sided appendicitis.

questionText: Meckel's diverticulum is a derivative of:
explanation:
Meckel's diverticulum is formed as a result of incomplete closure of omphalo-mesenteric duct or vitello-intestinal duct
Most commonly encountered anomaly of small intestine
Rule of 2: Prevalence in 2% population, 2 inch in length, 2 feet proximal to ileocaecal valve, symptomatic cases are < 2 years of age
Is a true diverticulum as it has all 3 layers of intestine and is located at the antimesenteric border of the ileum. Its caliber is equal to that of ileum.
20% cases have heterotopic tissues: Gastric mucosa (50%) followed by pancreatic mucosa (5%) and colonic mucosa (rarely)
Source of bleeding is ectopic gastric mucosa if present.
Most of them are entirely benign and incidentally discovered.
Presentation: GI bleeding (Most common clinical presentation seen by Tcm scanning in > 30% cases), intestinal obstruction due to band between apex and umbilicus (20-25% cases), diverticulitis (10-20%), intussusception, chronic ulceration, perforation
Most common complication in children and young adults is bleeding while most common complication in adults is intestinal obstruction.
When the appendix is found to be normal during exploration for suspected appendicitis, the distal ileum should be inspected for the presence of inflamed Meckel's diverticulum.
Diagnosis: Scintigraphy with sodium 99m Tc pertechnate is done for identification of heterotrophic gastric tissue and bleeding; enteroclysis (small bowel enema under fluoroscopy) is most accurate diagnostic test in children
Treatment:
1. Asymptomatic when found during abdominal surgery
i. Wide mouth, not thickened - do not remove
ii. Narrow mouth - remove
2. Diverticulitis: diverticulectomy (it should not be amputated at base and invaginated similar to appendix due to risk of stricture and leaving heterotopic epithelium behind)
i. Wedge resection
ii. If badly inflamed, friable, gangrenous and involves ileum: limited small bowel resection of involved segment, then end to end anastomosis.

questionText: Ramavtar, a 65 years-old man is admitted to the hospital with complaints of intermittent constipation and microcytic anemia. Barium enema reveals a non-obstructing apple-core lesion of proximal sigmoid colon. Colonoscopy confirms the location of the mass and reveals no other synchronous lesions. Treatment of choice is?
explanation:
The extent of resection is determined by the location of cancer, its blood supply and draining lymphatic system and the presence or absence of direct extension onto adjacent organs.
The procedure of choice for:
* Lesions involving the caecum, ascending colon, hepatic flexure or proximal transverse colon: right hemicolectomy followed by ileo-transverse colon anastomosis (removal of bowel from 4 to 6 cm proximal to ileocaecal valve to the portion of transverse colon supplied by the right branch of middle colic artery)
* Lesions involving transverse colon or splenic flexure: Extended right hemicolectomy (involves division of right and middle colic arteries at their origin with removal of right and transverse colon supplied by these vessels; anastomosis is done between the terminal ileum and proximal left colon)
* Lesions of descending colon: left hemicolectomy (resection from splenic flexure to rectosigmoid junction)
* Lesions of sigmoid colon: sigmoidectomy

questionText: A 63-year-old man is presently asymptomatic after medical treatment for LLQ pain and tenderness. He should undergo:
explanation: Colonoscopy is the investigation of choice to rule out the pathology in the lower GI tract.

questionText: Most common late complication of colostomy:
explanation: Most common late complications of both end and loop colostomy is parastomal hernia. Complications are more common in loop colostomy as compared to end colostomy.

questionText: Many patients with ulcerative colitis are operated upon electively with total abdominal colectomy, rectal mucosectomy, formation of a small intestinal reservoir, and ileoanal anastomosis. The most common postoperative complication of this operation is which of the following?
explanation: The major postoperative morbidity following restorative proctocolectomy is small bowel obstruction. Bowel obstruction rates requiring re-operation have been reported in 10% to 20% of most series of patients undergoing ileal pouch-anal anastomosis. Pelvic or wound infections have been reported to occur in 5% of patients undergoing ileoanal anastomosis, although the overall infection rate has been reduced to approximately 5% in several recent series. Conversion to a permanent ileostomy as a result of postoperative complications is observed in fewer than 5% of patients.

questionText: Early postoperative complication of ileostomy:
explanation: The early complication (that occurs within 30 days) is necrosis for colostomy and obstruction for ileostomy. Postoperative complications that occur with significant frequency in ileostomy are Nipple valve dysfunction, pouchitis, intestinal obstruction and fistula. Late complications of ileostomy are vitamin B12 deficiency anemia, stoma problems valve malfunction and prolapsed rectum.

questionText: Investigation of choice in Hirschsprung's disease is:
explanation:
Hirschsprung's disease is characterized by the congenital absence of intramural ganglion cells (aganglionosis due to failure of migration of vagal neural crest cells into the developing gut) and the presence of hypertrophic nerves in the distal large bowel. The affected gut is in spasm causing a functional bowel obstruction. The aganglionosis is restricted to the rectum and sigmoid colon in 75 per cent of patients (short segment), while it affects the entire colon and a portion of terminal ileum in 10 per cent (to talcolonic aganglionosis).
A transition zone exists between the dilated, proximal normally innervated bowel and the narrow, spastic aganglionic segment.
Hirschsprung's disease may be familial or associated with Down's syndrome or other genetic disorders.
Presentation:
* Neonatal period: Delayed (or failure) passage of meconium, abdominal distension and bilious vomiting.
* Childhood or adult: severe chronic constipation.
* Enterocolitis is a potentially fatal complication of the disease.
Diagnosis: rectal biopsy is diagnostic. A contrast enema may show the narrow aganglionic segment, a cone and the dilated proximal bowel.
Surgery aims to remove the aganglionic segment and pull-through' ganglionic bowel to the anus (e.g. Swenson, Duhamel, Soave and transanal procedures) and can be done in a single stage or in several stages after first establishing a proximal stoma in normally innervated bowel.

questionText: Earliest symptoms in acute appendicitis is:
explanation: Pain in acute appendicitis first appears in periumbilical region which then localizes to the right lower quadrant as the inflammatory process progresses to involve the parietal peritoneum overlying the appendix. The classic pattern of migratory pain is the most reliable symptom of acute appendicitis.

questionText: Acute appendicitis is most commonly associated with which of the following signs?
options: Anorexia, abdominal pain, and right lower quadrant tenderness
White blood cell count greater than 20,000 per cu. mm.
explanation: The clinical picture of acute appendicitis comprises of migratory RIF pain, anorexia, nausea or vomiting, tenderness in RIF, rebound tenderness in RIF and fever. The lab works show leukocytosis and shift to left (band cells of neutrophils in peripheral blood smears).

questionText: Which of the following most often initiates the development of acute appendicitis?
explanation: The majority of patients with acute appendicitis have an obstructed lumen that is due to either hyperplasia of the lymph follicles in the wall of the appendix or a fecolith. The obstruction creates a site where the bacteria in the lumen multiply rapidly, producing exotoxins and endotoxins that then ulcerate the mucosa, allowing pathogenic organisms to enter the wall of the appendix. An inflammatory process follows that can extend to the serosa, and penetration through the serosal layer causes generalized peritonitis.

questionText: Rovsings' sign is elicited by;
options: Pain in the right lower quadrant when palpatory pressure is exerted in the left lower quadrant
Pain in the right lower quadrant when palpatory pressure is exerted directly over the point of tenderness
Flexion-extension of the right lower extremity
explanation: Rovsing's sign is the pain in RIF when palpation is done in LIF.

questionText: The diagnosis of acute appendicitis is most difficult to establish in:
explanation:
It is very difficult to establish a firm diagnosis of acute appendicitis in an infant of 1 year or younger since the patient cannot provide a history or be helpful during the physical examination. It is rare to make a definitive diagnosis preoperatively in such infants, and in such cases the appendix is usually perforated at the time of operation. While appendicitis is somewhat more difficult to diagnose in the elderly because of the reduced response to inflammation; nevertheless, it is usually possible to make the diagnosis. With pregnant women it is wise to remember that the enlarging uterus in the last trimester dislocates the appendix higher in the abdomen and that the signs and symptoms follow this anatomic shift accordingly.
All these cases are also called as atypical appendicitis as the classical description of pain is not evident in these patients suffering from acute appendicitis.

questionText: Ochsner-Sherren regimen is for:
explanation:
Ochsner-Sherren regime is used for conservative management of appendicular lump. The strategy is based on the premise that inflammatory process is already localized and that inadvertent surgery is difficult and may be dangerous. It may be impossible to find the appendix and a fecal fistula may form.
The patient is allowed nothing by mouth, IV antibiotic are given and a regular charting of vital signs done 4-hourly and a fluid balance record maintained. The measurement of the mass is regularly recorded.
Clinical deterioration or evidence of peritonitis is an indication for early laparotomy. Other criteria for stopping conservative treatment of an appendix mass.
A rising pulse rate, episodes of vomiting, temperature and other deterioration in vital signs
Increasing or spreading abdominal pain
Increasing size of the mass.

questionText: Mucocele of the appendix is:
explanation:
Mucocele of appendix is an obstructive dilation by intraluminal accumulation of mucoid material. It is caused by one of the four process: retention cyst, mucosal hyperplasia, cystadenomas and cystadenocarcinoma.
Intact mucoceles < 2cm are almost always benign. Larger mucoceles are likely to be neoplastic.

questionText: The predominant organism cultured from the peritoneal fluid of a patient with acute unruptured appendicitis is:
explanation: The peritoneal fluid in association with acute unruptured appendicitis is sterile. So no organism will be isolated.

questionText: Visceral pain is typically:
options: Perceived to be in the midline
explanation:
Peritoneum is a continuous visceral and parietal layer. The nerve supply to each layer is separate. The visceral layer i.e., the layer surrounding all intraabdominal organs is supplied by autonomic nerves (sympathetic and parasympathetic) and the parietal peritoneum is supplied by somatic innervation (spinal nerves). The pathways relaying the sensation of pain differ for each layer and differ in quality as well. Visceral pain is characteristically dull, crampy, deep, aching and may involve sweating and nausea. Parietal pain is sharp, severe and persistent. Visceral organs have very little pain sensation due to stretching of the mesentery and stimulation of the parietal peritoneum cause severe pain.
Normal embryologic development of the abdominal viscera proceeds with bilateral midline autonomic innervation that results in visceral pain usually being perceived as arising from the midline. Epigastric pain is typical of foregut origin. Periumbilical pain signifies pain emanating from the midgut. Hypogastric or lower abdominal midline pain indicates a hindgut origin.

questionText: Which of the following statements regarding the vasculature of the colon and rectum is incorrect?
options: The middle colic artery is a branch of the superior mesenteric artery
The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the descending and sigmoid segments of the colon
An complete anastomotic arcade paralleling the colon wall is present in only 15 to 20% of individuals
The middle colic artery is a branch of the inferior mesenteric artery
explanation: Two major arterial systems supply the colon. The right colon is predominantly supplied by the superior mesenteric artery. The major branches of this artery that perfuse the right colon include the ileocolic branch, which supplies the ileocecal junction; the right colic, which supplies the ascending colon; and the middle colic artery, which supplies the hepatic flexure and the transverse colon to its midpoint. The left colon is predominantly supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery, which derives its origin from the abdominal aorta. The distal transverse colon and the descending colon obtain their blood supply from the left colic branch of the inferior mesenteric artery, while the sigmoid colon obtains its blood supply from sigmoidal branches. The colic arteries bifurcate and form vascular arcades so that the resultant marginal Drummond artery forms an anastomosis between the superior mesenteric artery and the inferior mesenteric artery. However, considerable anatomic variation exists with respect to this arterial arcade, and a complete anastomosis is present in only 15% to 20% of people.

questionText: A 65-year-old man presents with complaints of mucous discharge and perianal discomfort. Physical examination reveals a fistulous opening lateral to the anus. Anoscopic examination permits passage of a probe through the fistula tract. The fistula traverses the internal anal sphincter, the intersphincteric plane, and a portion of the external anal sphincter. The fistula is categorized as which type?
explanation: There are four main forms of fistula-in-ano, based on the relation of the fistula to the sphincter muscles. An intersphincteric fistula tract is in the intersphincteric plane. The external opening is usually in the perianal skin close to the anal verge. A transsphincteric fistula starts in the intersphincteric plane or in the deep postanal space. The fistulous track traverses the external sphincter, with the external opening at the ischioanal fossa. Horseshoe fistulas are in this category. Suprasphincteric fistulas start in the intersphincteric plane in the mid-anal canal and then pass upward to a point above the puborectalis. The fistula passes laterally over this muscle and downward between the puborectalis and the levator ani muscle into the ischioanal fossa. An extrasphincteric fistula passes from the perineal skin through the ischioanal fossa, the levator ani muscle, and finally penetrates the rectal wall. Extrasphincteric fistulas may arise from cryptoglandular origin, trauma, foreign body, or pelvic abscess.

questionText: Spontaneous closure of which of the following congenital abnormality of the abdominal wall generally occurs by the age of 4?
explanation: The umbilical defect/hernia is present at birth but closes as the stump of the umbilical cord heals, usually within a week of birth. This process may be delayed, leading to the development of herniation in the neonatal period. The umbilical ring may also stretch and reopen in adult life. This common condition occurs in up to 10 per cent of infants, with a higher incidence in premature babies. The hernia appears within a few weeks of birth and is often symptomless but increases in size on crying and assumes a classical conical shape. Sexes are equally affected but the incidence in black infants is up to eight times higher than in white. Obstruction and/or strangulation are extremely uncommon below the age of three years. Conservative treatment is indicated under the age of two years when the hernia is symptomless. Parental reassurance is all that is necessary. Ninety-five per cent of hernias will resolve spontaneously. If the hernia persists beyond the age of two years it is unlikely to resolve and surgical repair is indicated.

questionText: For differentiating inguinal hernia and femoral hernia, the landmark will be:
explanation: An inguinal hernia is positioned above the inguinal ligament and medial to the pubic tubercle, and femoral hernia lies below the inguinal ligament and lateral to the pubic tubercle. questionText: During surgery of hernia, the sac of a strangulated inguinal hernia should be opened at the:

questionText: Mayo's operation is done for:

Those that persist beyond 5 years need to be repaired surgically. Small defects are closed primarily while large defects > 3 cm are closed using prosthetic mesh. Mayo's repair employs imbrication of superior and inferior fascial edges. Because of the increased tension on repair and high recurrence rate of 30%, it is rarely performed now as days.

questionText: Hernia that is least likely to strangulate is:

questionText: Which of the following statements regarding splenic function in humans is true?
options: The specific immune function of the spleen is principally related to its antigen processing role
The spleen is the major site of synthesis of complement pathway proteins
The spleen is more efficient than the liver at removing bacteria with a high density of surface opsonins
The spleen serves as the only source of nonspecific opsonins
explanation:
Immune function of the spleen includes both nonspecific and specific immune responses. Nonspecific immune function is largely characterized by removal of particulate matter by the macrophages. The spleen contains 25% of the fixed tissue macrophage population in the body. The spleen is more efficient than the liver at removal of incompletely opsonized bacteria. The liver is most effective at removing bacteria with a high density of surface opsonins. The spleen also serves as a principal source of nonspecific opsonins. These include tuftsin, properidin, and fibronectin.
The specific immune functions of the spleen are principally related to its antigen-processing role, and this is in turn dependent on its unique anatomy and the circulation of lymphocytes into the spleen.
The liver, not the spleen, is the major site of synthesis of complement pathway proteins.

questionText: Which of the following doesn't fit in to definition of hypersplenism?

questionText: Most common cyst in spleen is:

questionText: In Couinaud's classification, segment IV of liver is:
explanation:
ANATOMY OF LIVER
Liver is divided into two lobes right and left by Cantlie's line (Extends from Gall bladder fossa to left side of IVC)
Falciform ligament divides left lobe into medial and lateral segment
Arterial supply of liver is by portal vein (75%) and hepatic artery (25%)
Venous drainage is by right, intermediate and left hepatic veins.
Couinaud's classification defined by branching of portal and hepatic vein in clockwise direction

| Segment | Location |
| --- | --- |
| Segment I | caudate |
| Segment II | left lateral superior |
| Segment III | left lateral inferior |
| Segment IV | left medial or quadrate |
| Segment V | right anterior inferior |
| Segment VI | right posterior inferior |
| Segment VII | right posterior superior |
| Segment VIII | right anterior superior |

Caudate lobe is unique as it:
* Lies between left portal vein and IVC
* Receives blood supply from both right and left portal pedicles
* Drains bile to both right and left hepatic ducts
* Venous drainage is directly to IVC.

Indications for aspiration:
* High risk of rupture (size more than 5 cms, left lobe abscess)
* Failure to respond with medical treatment in 3-5 days
* Pregnancy
* Pyogenic superinfection
Complications: rupture in peritoneum, pleural cavity or pericardium, requires surgery.

questionText: A 40 years male presents with a painless cystic liver enlargement of 4 years duration without fever or Jaundice. The most likely diagnosis is
explanation:
HYDATID CYST
Cause: A zoonosis, occurring primarily in sheep grazing areas of world, caused by Echinococcus Granulosus (Dog tape worm)
Definitive host: Dog; Usual intermediate host: Sheep, Humans are accidental dead end intermediate host. There is no human to human transmission.
Commonly involved organs: liver > lung > spleen > kidney > brain > Bone.
Most cysts in liver are single and located in right lobe.
Present with abdominal pain, dyspepsia and vomiting (MC symptoms) and hepatomegaly (most common sign)
Most common complication: Intrabiliary rupture of cyst. Other complications rupture into bronchial tree, peritoneal, pleural or pericardial cavities ruptures may result in fatal anaphylactic reaction.
USG and CT are the diagnostic modalities; confirmed by serological test (ELISA).
X-ray shows collapsed laminated membrane producing an irregular projections in a fluid level due to rupture of the cyst - Water-lily appearance.
Positive Casoni's test.
Treatment options:
Conservative management - elderly patients, with small, asymptomatic, densely calcified cyst
PAIR (Puncture, Aspiration of cyst content, Injection of scolicidal agent and Reaspiration) is the preferred method for anatomically and surgically appropriate lesions. Contraindicated in cyst with communication with biliary tree.
Surgery it the treatment of choice when PAIR is not possible or cysts are refractory to PAIR and for complicated cysts. Pericystectomy is the preferred surgical approach. If cystectomy is not technically feasible, liver resection can be done.
Chemotherapy with Albendazole is effective in shrinking the cysts.
Treatments of E. multilocularis (Which is always multiloculated) is surgical resection.

questionText: A 40 years old male presents with hematemesis. On examination his BP was 90/60 mm Hg and heart rate was 120/min. Splenomegaly was also present. The most probable cause of his bleeding is:
explanation:
Presence of splenomegaly in a patient with GI bleeding points to portal hypertension.
Management of bleeding oesophageal varices:
* Blood transfusion
* Correct coagulopathy
* Oesophageal balloon tamponade (Sengstaken-Blakemore tube)
* Drug therapy (vasopressin/octreotide)
* Endoscopic sclerotherapy or banding
* Assess portal vein patency (Doppler ultrasound or CT)
* Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic stent shunts (TIPSS)
* Surgery
  * Portosystemic shunts
  * Oesophageal transection
  * Splenectomy and gastric devascularisation

questionText: Which of the following agents is recommended for medical treatment of variceal bleed?
explanation: Somatostatin or its analog octreotide are the drug of choice for medical management of variceal bleed. TIPSS stands for Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic stent shunts.

questionText: In Budds-Chiari syndrome, the occlusion is at the
explanation:
Budd-Chiari Syndrome
Caused by obstruction of hepatic venous outflow producing intense congestion of liver and the classic manifestation of ascites, hepatomegaly and abdominal pain.
Polycythemia rubra vera is the most common etiology.

questionText: Multiple liver secondaries are most common in the following cancers:
explanation: Gall bladder carcinoma is associated with massive palpable secondaries in the liver.

questionText: Most common liver tumor in those on OCPs?
explanation: Hepatic adenoma is a benign proliferative disorder of hepatocytes, predominantly found in young women (20-40 years) associated with OCPs.

questionText: Normal diameter of CBD is:
explanation: Normal diameter of CBD is 6-8 mm. It is seen as dilated (> 10 mm) in case of CBD stones, which is a diagnostic finding in USG.

questionText: Percentage of gall stones which are radio opaque:
explanation: 90% Gall stones are radiolucent. 90% Renal stones are radiopaque.

questionText: A gall stone gets impacted most commonly in which part of common bile duct?
explanation: The gall stone that travels along the common bile duct gets impacted at the ampulla of vater.

questionText: A 45-years old female presents with symptoms of acute cholecystitis. On USG there is a solitary gallstone of size 1.5 cms. Symptoms are controlled with medical management. Which of the following is the next most appropriate step in management of this patient?
explanation:
MANAGEMENT OF ACUTE CHOLECYSTITIS
Early cholecystectomy performed within 2-3 days of presentation is preferred over interval or delayed cholecystectomy after initial medical therapy.
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is preferred approach to patients with acute cholecystitis.
Absolute contraindications for laparoscopic cholecystectomy are:
* unable to tolerate GA,
* refractory coagulopathy,
* suspicion of carcinoma.
Relative contraindications for laparoscopic cholecystectomy include:
* previous upper abdominal surgery,
* cholangitis,
* diffuse peritonitis,
* cirrhosis or portal hypertension,
* COPD,
* cholecystenteric fistula,
* morbid obesity and
* pregnancy.
Indications of open cholecystectomy include:
* Poor pulmonary or cardiac reserve,
* Cirrhosis and pulmonary hypertension
* Combined procedure
* Suspected or known gallbladder cancer
* Third trimester pregnancy

questionText: Internal fistula is most common between gall bladder and:
explanation:
GALL STONE ILEUS
Passage of a gall stone through a spontaneous biliary-enteric fistula leading to mechanical bowel obstruction.
Most common site of fistula is between gall bladder and 1st part of duodenum.
Clinical features: Small bowel obstruction, pneumobilia and ectopic gallstone (Rigler's triad)
Most common site of obstruction is ileum followed by jejunum, stomach, colon, sigmoid colon and duodenum.
It is a surgical emergency.

questionText: What is the appropriate treatment for an incidental 3 cm liver hemangioma found on abdominal CT scan of 37 year old woman?
options: Selective embolization of left hepatic artery
explanation: Hemangioma of the liver are the benign tumors of the liver. It is mainly the incidental finding during USG of abdomen. It has very little or no malignant potential. Size <8 cm are not associated with complication. So wait and watch is best policy.

questionText: Indications of prophylactic cholecystectomy are all except:
explanation:
Diabetes is not an indication for prophylactic cholecystectomy.
Indications of prophylactic cholecystectomy:
* Cardiac transplant and lung transplant recipients
* Chronic TPN requirement
* Children with hemoglobinopathies (Sickle cell, thalassemia and spherocytosis)
* Asymptomatic gallstone >3cm
* Stone associated with a polyp
* Family history of GB cancer
* Nonfunctioning GB
* Typhoid carrier with positive bile culture
* Trauma to GB
* Porcelain GB

questionText: The treatment of choice for a mucocele of gall bladder is:
explanation:
Mucocele or hydrops of GB results from prolonged obstruction of the cystic duct usually by a large solitary calculus. The obstructed GB lumen is progressive distended by mucus (mucocele) or by a clear fluid (hydrops) produced by mucosal epithelial cells.
Visible, easily palpable, non-tender gall bladder is the clinical feature, often patient is asymptomatic. Early cholecystectomy is the treatment of choice as empyema, perforation or gangrene may complicate the situation.

questionText: Mirizzi syndrome is:
options: GB stone compressing common hepatic duct
explanation: Mirizzi syndrome: Obstruction of the common hepatic duct or CBD by external compression or by erosion of stone in Hartmann's pouch or cystic duct.

questionText: Precancerous lesions of GB are all except:
explanation:
Risk factors for CA Gall bladder:
* Gall stone > 3cm
* Porcelain gall bladder
* Anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction
* Choledochal cysts
* Adenomatous polyps
* Primary sclerosing cholangitis
* Obesity
* Salmonella typhi infection

questionText: Sentinel node of gall bladder is
explanation:
Important lymph nodes:
* Rotter's Node: Interpectoral nodes (CA breast)
* Rouvier node: Retropharyngeal nodes (CA nasopharynx)
* Delphian nodes: Pre-cricoid lymph nodes
* Irish nodes: Nodes in left axilla (CA stomach)
* Sister Mary Joseph nodes: Periumbilical metastatic cutaneous nodules.
* Virchow nodes: Left supraclavicular nodes
* Cloquet node: Femoral canal
* Lymph node of Lund: Cystic lymph nodes
* Krause LN: Jugular Fossa LN

questionText: Best test to differentiate between medical and surgical jaundice is?
explanation: Hepatic and pre-hepatic jaundice are medical jaundice and obstructive jaundice is the surgical jaundice. USG of hepatobiliary and pancreatic system is the best test to differentiate between the two.

questionText: Best treatment modality for common bile duct stone is
explanation: Endoscopic clearance of CBD stones can avoid the need for an open operation. Complete clearance is achieved in 71-75% of patients at first procedure and 84%-95% of patients after multiple endoscopic procedure.

questionText: A middle aged patients presents with complain of right hypochondrial pain. On x-ray, elevated right hemi-diaphragm was seen. All of the following are the possible diagnosis except?
options: Amoebic liver abscess in right lobe
explanation:
[ Causes of elevated hemidiaphragm ]
   ↓
├── Above the diaphragm
│   ├── Decreased lung volume:
│   │   ├── Atelectasis/ Collapse
│   │   ├── Lobectomy/ pneumonectomy
│   │   └── Pulmonary hypoplasia
│   └── Phrenic nerve palsy
│       ├── Diaphragmatic eventration
│       └── Contralateral CVA
└── Below the diaphragm
    ├── Abdominal tumor
    ├── Subphrenic abscess
    └── Liver abscess (Amoebic / pyogenic)

questionText: Caroli's disease is:
explanation: Caroli's disease is type V choledochal cyst where dilation is confined to intrahepatic bile ducts. Choledochal cysts: Cystic dilation of the biliary ducts, common in females.

questionText: Most common cause of cholangitis:
explanation: Cholangitis is the infection of the bile duct characterized by fever, jaundice, pain and in confusion and shock. Bile duct obstruction is the main cause of cholangitis. The main cause is stone in CBD. Other causes include, benign stricture, operative trauma, carcinoma of CBD, etc.

questionText: In cholangitis, the organism mostly responsible is
explanation: The common organisms associated with cholangitis Gram negative rods; E. coli (25-50%), Klebsiella (15-20%), Enterobacter and Gram positive cocci like Enterococcus.

questionText: The following is not a feature of common bile duct stones:
explanation:
Courvoisier's law states that "in a jaundiced patient if the gall bladder is palpable & non-tender, it is unlikely to be gallstones". It is so because previous inflammation will have made gallbladder fibrotic, thick and non-distensible and thus in case of stones, the gall bladder enlargement is not found. The law indirectly explains that such a palpable GB is likely due to carcinoma.
Exceptions to Courvoisier's law are:
* Double impaction of stones occluding cystic duct and CBD
* Oriental cholangiohepatitis
* Pancreatic calculi obstructing ampulla
* Mucocele or empyema GB
* Periampullary carcinoma in a patient who has undergone cholecystectomy

questionText: Which of the following is not a part of Charcot's triad?
explanation: Charcot's triad is the feature of acute cholangitis; intermittent pain in RUQ, fever and jaundice. Charcot's triad with shock and confusion is called Reynold's pentad.

questionText: A 50 years old woman presented with history of recurrent episodes of right upper quadrant pain for last one year. She presented to the casualty with history of jaundice and fever for 4 days. On examination, the patient appeared toxic and a blood pressure of 90/60 mm of Hg. She was started on IV antibiotics. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed presence of stones in CBD. What would be the best treatment for her?
options: Open surgery and bile duct stone extraction
explanation: CBD stones with features of cholangitis is best managed by open surgery with bile duct exploration (T-tube cholangiogram) and removal of the CBD stones.

questionText: After exploration of common bile duct, the T-tube is removed on which of the following days:
explanation:
T-tube cholangiogram is done on 8-10th day (water soluble dye is injected into the tube and X-ray is taken). Complete free flow of dye into the duodenum indicates that there is no blockage. T-tube can then be removed safely after further 2-4 days. Block indicates residual CBD stones.
After choledochotomy, Kehr's T-tube is placed in CBD for 12-14 days, by which the track is well formed; even if minor leak is present, it flows without causing peritonitis.

questionText: The earliest symptom in primary biliary cirrhosis is:
explanation:
Primary biliary cirrhosis:
* Believed to be autoimmune in etiology, leading to progressive destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts.
* More common in females.
* Associated with autoimmune disorders (CREST, SICCA syndrome, autoimmune thyroiditis, renal tubular acidosis)
* Most patients are asymptomatic, pruritus is the commonest and earliest symptom and occurs before jaundice.
* S. Bilirubin is the best guide to prognosis.
* Mainstay of treatment of pruritus is cholestyramine.

questionText: Fluctuating non painful jaundice with waxing & waning pattern is suggestive of:
explanation: In periampullary carcinoma sometimes necrosis of tumor occurs as a result of which jaundice may reduce temporarily thus being intermittent. (Waxing & waning)

questionText: The neck of pancreas is related on its posterior surface to:
explanation: The posterior surface of pancreas is related to the portal vein.

questionText: A lady presents with three days history of epigastric pain radiating to back. Serum amylase levels were observed to be normal while USG abdomen revealed CBD stones and an enlarged pancreas. CT scan was done which clinched the diagnosis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Acute abdomen with features of epigastric pain radiating to back is seen in acute pancreatitis. In acute pancreatitis, pancreas may be edematous and gall stone or CBD stone may be seen as it is the common cause of acute pancreatitis. Serum amylase may be raised or may be normal (in about 10% cases).

questionText: The commonest cause of acute pancreatitis is:
explanation:
Causes of acute pancreatitis:
* Gall stones (most common)
* Alcohol (2nd most common)
* Hypertriglyceridemia
* Post-ERCP
* Blunt abdominal traumas
* Drugs (corticosteroids, azathioprine, asparaginase, valproic acid, thiazides, estrogens)
* Infections (CMV, Coxsackie, Mumps)
* Autoimmune (Sjogren's syndrome)
* Cystic fibrosis
* TTP
* Hypercalcemia

questionText: Which of the following is most diagnostic investigation for acute pancreatitis?
explanation: Serum amylase is the common test done in acute pancreatitis. Serum lipase is the best test and most specific test for acute pancreatitis. Serum lipase rises 4 to 8 hrs from the onset of the symptoms. Serum amylase may be normal or may be false positively raised as in cholecystitis, bowel obstruction, salivary gland disease, perforated ulcer.

questionText: Medical treatment of acute pancreatitis includes:
explanation:
Medical treatment of acute pancreatitis:
* Analgesics
* IV fluid and colloids
* Nil per oral
* Antibiotics
* Treatment of hypocalcaemia, if symptomatic

questionText: Cullen's sign is:
explanation:
Signs indicative of retroperitoneal bleeding in severe pancreatitis:
* Flank ecchymosis: Grey turner sign
* Periumbilical ecchymosis: Cullen's sign
* Inguinal ecchymosis: Fox sign

questionText: Most common symptom of chronic pancreatitis is:
explanation:
Abdominal pain is the primary manifestation and most common symptom of chronic pancreatitis.
If a patient resorts to the knee-elbow position to get relief from pain, it indicates that the pain is of pancreatic origin.

questionText: Most common complication of pseudocyst:
explanation: The commonest complication of acute pancreatitis is pseudocyst of pancreas, seen after 4-6 weeks of acute attack.

questionText: All of the following are true about pseudopancreatic cyst of pancreas except:
options: Most common site is in head of pancreas
explanation: Pseudocyst of pancreas is localized collection of sequestered pancreatic fluid, usually occurs 3-4 weeks after an attack of acute pancreatitis. It can occur after trauma and recurrent chronic pancreatitis. Collection usually occurs in the lesser sac (most common) in relation to stomach, but can occur in relation to duodenum, jejunum, colon, splenic hilum. About 50% of acute pancreatitis leads to pseudocyst formation among that 20-40% will resolve spontaneously.

questionText: Treatment of choice for asymptomatic pseudocyst of pancreas is:
explanation:
In case of pseudocyst of pancreas, the asymptomatic size less than 6 cm indicates that one can wait for spontaneous resolution.
Indications for surgery/intervention:
* Size more than 6 cm
* Infected pseudocyst
* Cyst persisting after 6 weeks/progressive cyst
* Multiple cysts/cyst due to trauma
* Communicating cysts/cyst with severe pain
* Thick walled pseudocyst
The surgical procedures done are:
* Cysto-gastrostomy
* Cysto-duodenostomy
* Endoscopic cysto-gastric stenting
* Laparoscopic cystogastrostomy is becoming popular, effective and less invasive.
* U/S guided aspiration is useful in initial phases.
* Distal pancreatectomy with pseudocyst removal if cyst is in distal part

questionText: Most sensitive investigation of pancreatic carcinoma is:
explanation: Investigation of choice of carcinoma pancreas is CT scan.

questionText: Components of Whipple's operation are following except:
explanation:
Whipple's procedure consists of complete removal of pancreatic head, hepatoduodenal ligament & lymph nodes, C-loop of duodenum with a short segment (10 cm) of the proximal jejunum, gall bladder & lower CBD, and the distal half to two thirds of the stomach with the right half of the greater omentum.
Restoration of GI continuity requires reconstruction in the order of:
1. Pancreatico-jejunostomy (PJ)
2. Choledocho-jejunostomy (CJ)
3. Gastro-jejunostomy (GJ)
Duodeno-jejunostomy is done in PPPD (pylorus preserving pancreatico-duodenectomy) not in Whipple's procedure.

questionText: All of the following statements regarding Whipple's procedure are true, except:
options: Duodenum is resected along with pancreatic head due to the common blood supply
Without sphincter of Oddi, filling of GB with bile is not possible, hence it is resected
Distal (pyloric) stomach is resected because it contains the lymph nodes which commonly get local spread from the pancreatic head tumor
explanation:
Pancreatic head and duodenum have common blood supply in the form of pancreaticoduodenal artery.
Retrograde filling occurs in GB. The bile from the common hepatic duct drains down to the sphincter of Oddi and then fills the GB in retrograde fashion.
Distal (pyloric) stomach contains abundant lymph nodes which commonly get local spread from the pancreatic head tumor.

questionText: ERCP reveals a periampullary cancer in a 64-year-old man admitted for jaundice. No metastasis is detected; no co-morbid conditions are identified. How should he be managed?
options: Radical excision of the head of pancreas and duodenum
explanation: In cases of operable tumors of pancreas, the standard resection for a tumour of the pancreatic head or the ampulla is a pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy. Whipple procedure is also another modality of surgery. Periampullary carcinoma includes a group of malignant tumors arising at or near the ampulla, adenocarcinoma from head of pancreas adjacent to the ampulla (within 2 cm)—40-60%, ampullary tumor arising from ampulla of Vater—20-40%, distal bile duct carcinoma—10% and duodenal carcinoma adjacent to the ampulla—10%.

questionText: All of the following surgical procedures are appropriate for a patient who has a pseudocyst of head of pancreas, except:
options: Removal of involved segment of pancreas
explanation:
The surgical procedures done in case of pseudocyst of pancreas are:
* Cysto-gastrostomy
* Cysto-duodenostomy
* Cystojejunostomy
* Endoscopic cysto-gastric stenting
* External drainage
* Laparoscopic cystogastrostomy is becoming popular, effective and less invasive
* U/S guided aspiration is useful in initial phases
* Distal pancreatectomy with pseudocyst removal if cyst is in distal part

questionText: Which of the following is not a component of syndrome X?
explanation:
When 3 or more of these are present, it is termed as Syndrome X (Insulin resistance syndrome or Reaven's syndrome):
* Fasting glucose >110 but <126 mg/dl
* Blood pressure >130/85 mmHg
* Triglycerides > 150 mg/dl
* HDL in plasma <50 mg/dl

questionText: Which of the following is not true about surgical jaundice?
options: Appearance of pain before jaundice is distinctive feature than medical jaundice
Triple bypass surgery is a palliative surgery
Sphincterotomy is done for CBD stones
explanation:
Biochemical features of different types of jaundice:

| Type of jaundice | Haemolytic | Early | Late | Obstructive |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Serum bilirubin | ↑ | N/↑ | N/↑ | N |
| Unconjugated | N | N | ↑ | ↑↑ |
| Conjugated | N/↑ | ↑ | ↑ | ↑↑ |
| Urinary bilirubin | N/↑ | N | ↑ | ↑↑ |
| Urobilinogen | - | - | - | - |
| LFTs | N | N | ↑ | ↑↑ |
| Alkaline phosphatase | N | ↑ | ↑ | ↑↑ |
| γ- GT transaminase | N | ↑ | ↑↑ | N/↑ |
| Transaminases | N | ↑ | ↑↑ | N/↑ |
| Lactate dehydrogenase | - | - | - | - |
| FBC | N | N | N | N |
| Reticulocyte | >2% | - | - | - |

questionText: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is characterized by all of the following except:
options: Massive HCl secretion in response to histamine injection
explanation:
Clinical features of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome:
* Gastric acid hypersecretion leading to peptic ulcer disease, often refractory
* Severe diarrhea
* Most common presenting symptoms abdominal pain, diarrhea and GERD.

questionText: Anatomical description for a level 1 lymph node in breast is:
options: Below and lateral to the pectoralis major
Below and lateral to the pectoralis minor
Above and medial to pectoralis minor
Above and medial to pectoralis major
explanation:
The axillary lymph nodes are described in 3 levels, defined by the relationship to the pectoralis minor muscle.
Level 1: Below and lateral to lateral margin of pectoralis minor, consists of anterior, lateral and posterior group of axillary lymph nodes
Level II: Posterior to pectoralis minor; consists of central group of axillary lymph nodes
Level III: Above and medial to pectoralis minor; consists of apical group of axillary lymph nodes
Anterior group, also called as pectoral or external mammary node, is the main drainage node. Similarly posterior group, also called as subscapular node, rarely involves in carcinoma. Additional lymph nodes (called Rotter nodes) can be identified in the interpectoral space between the pectoralis major and minor muscles.

questionText: Best diagnostic method for breast lump is:
explanation: Biopsy is the best diagnostic method for breast lump.

questionText: A female patient present with a hard mobile lump in her right breast. Which initial investigation would be most helpful in making the diagnosis?
explanation:
First investigation of choice in breast carcinoma is FNAC
Best diagnostic test is Biopsy

questionText: A lady 35 years old lactating mother presented with a painful breast lump. Most appropriate initial investigation should be:
explanation:
Indication for USG in breast:
* Symptomatic breast lump in women <35 years (more dense breast tissue)
* Breast lump during lactation and pregnancy (denser breast tissue)
* Clinical breast mass with negative mammogram
* Breast inflammation
* Guidance of needle biopsy or localization.

questionText: True about screening mammography:
options: Radiation due to mammography can cause carcinoma
explanation:
Mammography:
Soft tissue radiographs are taken by placing the breast in direct contact with ultrasensitive film and exposing it to low-voltage, high amperage x-rays. The dose of radiation is approximately 0.1 cGy (By comparison chest radiography delivers 25% of this dose) and, therefore, mammography is a very safe investigation.
Screening mammography uses two views:
1. Craniocaudal (CC) view provides better visualization of the medial aspect of the breast and permits greater tissue compression
2. Mediolateral oblique (MLO) view images the greatest volume of breast tissue, including the upper & outer quadrant and the axillary tail of Spence.
The sensitivity of this investigation increases with age as the breast becomes less dense. In total, 5 per cent of all cancers are missed by population-based mammographic screening programs; even in retrospect, such carcinomas are not apparent. Thus, a normal mammogram does not exclude the presence of carcinoma.
Starting at the age of 40 years, breast examinations should be performed yearly and yearly mammogram should be taken. There is no increased risk of breast cancer associated with a radiation dose of screening mammography.

questionText: Blood stained nipple discharge is seen in:
explanation:
Discharges from the nipple (the principal causes are in bold):
a) Discharge from the surface:
* Paget's disease
* Skin diseases (eczema, psoriasis)
b) Blood stained:
* Intraductal papilloma (about 60% of blood stained discharge)
* Intraductal carcinoma
c) Serous (any colour):
* Fibrocystic disease
* Duct ectasia
* Carcinoma
d) Black or green: Duct ectasia
e) Purulent: infection
f) Milk: lactation or rarely hypothyroidism or pituitary tumor
Nipple discharge may be suggestive of cancer if it is spontaneous, unilateral, localized to a single duct, present in women ≥40 years of age, bloody, or associated with a mass.
Nipple discharge is suggestive of a benign condition if it is bilateral and multiductal in origin, occurs in women ≤39 years of age, or is milky or blue-green.

questionText: The reason why approximately one half of breast cancer are located at the upper outer quadrant is
options: The larger volume of breast tissue
explanation: Although any portion of the breast, including the axillary tail, may be involved, breast cancer is found most frequently in the upper outer quadrant due to the larger volume of breast tissue.

questionText: True about Paget's disease of the nipple is:
options: Often bilateral eczema of nipple seen
explanation:
PAGETS DISEASE
It is the superficial manifestation of underlying breast carcinoma, in which Malignant cells are seen in subdermal layer.
Pathogenesis: expansion of DCIS upto lactiferous duct and contiguous skin of nipple (without crossing basement membrane) - disrupts squamous epithelium barrier.
Presents as eczema like condition of nipple and areola which persists despite local treatment.
Nipple is eroded slowly and eventually disappears.
Biopsy: Paget's cells (large ovoid and abundant with clear pale staining cytoplasm) in malpighian layer of epidermis.

questionText: A smooth rubbery 3 cm lesion is removed from the breast of 35-year-old woman with a preoperative diagnosis of fibroadenoma. Histologically, this lesion is found to be phyllode tumor. Appropriate management at this time is:
options: Re-excision of area with a 1 cm margin
explanation: Small phyllode tumors are excised with a 1 cm margin of normal appearing breast tissue.

questionText: Most frequent site of accessory breast:
explanation: Polymastia or accessory breasts have been recorded in the axilla (mc site), groin, buttock and high along the milk line. They have been known to function during lactation.

questionText: Mondor's disease is:
options: Thrombophlebitis of the superficial veins of breast
explanation:
Mondor's disease is a variant thrombophlebitis of superficial veins of breast and anterior chest wall (may be seen in arm). Frequently involved veins include the lateral thoracic vein, the thoraco-epigastric vein, and, less commonly, the superficial epigastric vein. It is also known as string phlebitis as a thrombosed vein presents as a tender, cord like structure. This is a benign self-limited condition, not indicative of cancer. Cause is unknown (may be injury or infection).
Clinical features:
* Thrombosed subcutaneous cord, attached to skin
* On raising the arm: narrow, shallow subcutaneous groove
* D/D: lymphatic permeation from an occult carcinoma of breast
Treatment is with NSAIDS and application of warm compress with restricted arm movements.

questionText: A 20-year-old woman consults for a 2-cm mass in her left breast. The mass is movable, non-tender and has a rubbery consistency and smooth borders. The probable diagnosis is:
explanation: Fibroadenoma is a benign encapsulated tumor occurring commonly in young females of 15-25 years age group. It is considered as hyperplasia of a single lobule of the breast (classified under ANDI). It is the most common benign tumor of the breast. It presents as a painless swelling in one of the quadrants, which is smooth, firm, nontender, well localized and moves freely within the breast tissue (mouse in the breast).

questionText: A lactating female presented with breast abscess. Most common organism responsible for her mastitis and abscess formation is:
explanation:
Bacterial mastitis (Lactational mastitis) are typically staphylococcal infection.
Predisposing factors: nipple crack or bite, inverted nipple, oral cavity infection of child: 50% of infants harbor Staphylococci after 2nd day of life, which leads to ascending infection during lactation and in the ampulla, staphylococci clots the blood, and multiplication of organism occurs.
Clinical features:
a. Stage of cellulitis: Spreading inflammation; Throbbing pain, fever, Red hot tender breast, Non-fluctuant swelling
b. Stage of suppuration (abscess): Localization of inflammation, High grade fever with chills and rigors, Soft, cystic with fluctuant swelling (late sign), Increase breast size, brawny edema
Treatment:
a. Cellulitic stage: Antibiotic: Flucloxacillin/Co-amoxiclav (add metron for non-lactational); Rest to breast by not feeding (decompress milk by pump); Breast support, local heat and analgesia. If does not resolve by 48 hours: Incision and drainage
b. Abscess: Repeated aspiration under USG guidance under antibiotic cover, and pus culture, OR
c. Incision and drainage: If does not resolve in 48 hours or tense induration after emptying milk; or, after repeated aspiration and antibiotics; or, thinning or necrosis of the overlying skin
i. Under LA after applying EMLA for 30 minutes, radial incision - skin and fascia - long artery forcep - finger pack with ribbon gauze or place a drain in biodependent area. Abscess cavity wall should be considered at the time of incision and drainage to rule out underlying breast cancer in patients where antibiotics and drainage have been ineffective.

questionText: Lymphangiosarcoma secondary to chronic lymphedema following axillary dissection is:
explanation: Stewart Treves syndrome is an angiosarcoma developing in patients with chronic lymphedema of the upper limb after mastectomy with lymph node dissection. Diagnosis is confirmed with biopsy.

questionText: A woman noticed mass in her left breast with bloody discharge. Histopathology revealed duct ectasia. Treatment is:
explanation:
Duct ectasia/Periductal mastitis
Dilatation of breast ducts associated with periductal inflammation
Common in middle aged woman and smokers, May have low grade anaerobic infection
Clinical features:
1. Nipple discharge (of any color)
2. Subareolar mass
3. Abscess (subareolar): Unlike puerperal abscesses, a subareolar abscess is usually unilocular and often is associated with a single duct system
4. Mammary duct fistula: Rx fistulectomy and primary closure with antibiotic coverage
5. Slit like nipple retraction
Treatment:
1. Antibiotics: fluclox/co-amoxiclav plus metron
2. Surgery: excision of all major ducts (Hadfields operation), shave back of nipple to remove all terminal ducts which prevents recurrence
3. Cessation of smoking

questionText: Which of the following is a predisposing factor to breast cancer?
explanation:

questionText: Which one predisposes to breast cancer?
explanation: Epitheliosis (Epithelial hyperplasia) predisposes to breast cancer.

questionText: Histological variety of breast carcinoma with best prognosis is:
explanation: Distant metastases are rare in tubular carcinoma and long term survival approaches 100%.

questionText: Bilateral, multicentric type of carcinoma in breast is usually:
explanation:
Lobular carcinoma in situ / Invasive lobular carcinoma:
LCIS is multicentric and bilateral.
Originates from terminal duct lobular units.
There is increased risk of invasive carcinoma in both breasts.

questionText: Which of the following indicate carcinoma breast?
explanation:
Cutaneous Manifestations of Carcinoma Breast:
* Peau d'orange: Due to obstruction of dermal lymphatics buried in the edema giving rise to orange peel appearance openings of the sebaceous glands and hair follicles
* Dimpling of skin due to infiltration of ligament of Cooper
* Retraction of nipple due to infiltration of lactiferous ducts
* Ulceration, discharge from the nipple and areola
* Skin ulceration and fungation.
* Cancer-en-cuirasse: Skin over the chest wall and breast is studded with cancer nodules appearing like an armour coat.
* Tethering to skin

questionText: Peau-d-orange' appearance of the mammary skin is due to:
explanation: Peau-d-orange is due to cutaneous lymphatic edema, wherein infiltrated skin is tethered by sweat ducts. It is due to obstruction of subdermal lymphatics and is seen in advanced breast cancer, may also be seen in chronic abscess.

questionText: Most common site of metastasis from breast carcinoma:
explanation:
Spread of breast cancer:
1. Direct spread:
i. Skin: ulceration, fungation, bleeding, foul smelling discharge
ii. Pectoralis muscle
iii. Chest wall
2. Lymphatic:
i. Axillary
ii. Parasternal (mediastinum and opposite breast)
iii. Internal mammary (posterior 1/3rd of breast)
3. Hematogenous: (via axillary vein, internal thoracic vein and posterior intercostal vein & paravertebral venous plexus)
a. Skeletal (osteolytic): lumbar vertebra > femur > thoracic vertebra > rib > skull
b. Lungs: cannon ball deposits, malignant pleural effusion
c. Liver, brain
4. Transcoelomic: (penetrate rectus sheath intraperitoneal lymphatics)
a. Malignant ascites
b. Ovary: krukenberg tumor
c. Blummer's shelf

questionText: Breast cancer is relatively common in:
explanation:
Risk factors for breast carcinoma:
* Breast carcinoma in 1st degree relative
* Breast carcinoma in contralateral breast
* BRCA1/BRCA2 gene mutation
* Obesity and alcohol intake
* Gynaecomastia in male breast
* Nulliparity
* Early menarche and late menopause

questionText: In Patey's modified mastectomy, which of the following is preserved?
explanation:
Types of breast surgery:
1. Radical (Halsted): breast + axillary LN + pectoralis major and minor
2. Modified radical (Patey): whole breast skin overlying tumor and nipple + fat, fascia and LN of axilla; division or retraction of pectoralis minor to gain access to upper 2/3rd of axilla (pectoralis major is preserved)
3. Simple mastectomy: only breast and axillary tail
4. Wide local excision: tumor plus rim of ≥1 cm of normal breast tissue
5. Quadrantectomy: entire segment of breast that contains tumor
6. Lumpectomy is done for benign tumor excision without normal tissue

questionText: Breast conservation surgery includes all of the following except:
explanation: The breast conservation surgery includes, wide excision, quadrantectomy with radiotherapy and axillary lymph node dissection, toilet mastectomy, skin sparing mastectomy, lumpectomy, and sentinel lymph node biopsy.

questionText: A 50 years old female has under gone mastectomy for CA breast. After mastectomy patient is not able to extend adduct and internally rotate the arm. Now supply to which of the following muscle is damaged?
explanation: Latissimus dorsi is active in adduction, extension and especially in medial rotation of humerus.

questionText: Postoperative radiotherapy in breast is given for
options: For ablation of remnant of cancer tissue
explanation: Radiotherapy to breast: after mastectomy for patients with high risk of local recurrence (large tumor and large positive nodes); radiotherapy is given to remaining breast tissue (not to axilla) to prevent recurrence.

questionText: Prognosis of metastatic breast cancer depends mostly upon:
explanation:
Best prognostic factors:
* Carcinoma breast: Stage Axillary LN status
* Metastatic Carcinoma breast: Hormone receptor (ER, PR) status
* Wilm's tumor: Histology

questionText: Gynaecomastia may be seen in patient with all except:
explanation:
Gynecomastia refers to an enlarged breast in the male. In the nonobese male, breast tissue measuring at least 2 cm in diameter must be present before a diagnosis of gynecomastia may be made.
Causes:
1. Physiological:
a. Neonatal
b. Adolescence: the condition often is unilateral and typically occurs between ages 12 and 15 years
c. Senescence
2. Estrogen deficiency states:
a. Gonadal origin: True hermaphroditism, Gonadal stromal (nongerminal) neoplasms of the testis, Germ cell tumors
b. Nontesticular tumors: Adrenal cortical neoplasms, Lung carcinoma, Hepatocellular carcinoma
c. Endocrine disorders
d. Diseases of the liver-nonalcoholic and alcoholic cirrhosis
e. Nutrition alteration states
3. Androgen deficiency states:
a. Senescence
b. Hypoandrogenic states (hypogonadism)
c. Primary testicular failure e.g., Klinefelter's syndrome (XXY)
d. Secondary testicular failure: Trauma, Orchitis, Cryptorchidism, Irradiation
e. Leprosy: bilateral testicular atrophy
4. Renal failure
5. Pharmacologic causes:
a. Drugs with estrogenic activity (digitalis, estrogens, anabolic steroids, marijuana)
b. Drugs that inhibit the action or synthesis of testosterone (cimetidine, ketoconazole, phenytoin, spironolactone, antineoplastic agents, diazepam)
c. Drugs such as reserpine, theophylline, verapamil, tricyclic antidepressants, and furosemide through idiopathic mechanisms
6. Systemic diseases with idiopathic mechanisms

questionText: In breast Ca, invasion of which of the muscles is not regarded as chest wall invasion?
explanation:
Knowledge of pectoral or chest wall invasion by breast cancer prior to surgery is important because of impact on tumor staging, surgical planning & overall therapeutic approach.
Chest wall invasion is defined as tumor infiltration of intercostal muscles and/or serratus anterior muscle.

questionText: Most common solitary thyroid nodule is:
explanation: Most common solitary thyroid nodule is colloid goiter (60%) followed by follicular adenoma (30%)[cite: 1].

questionText: What is the most appropriate operation for a solitary nodule in one lobe of thyroid?
options: d. Partial lobectomy with 1 cm margin around nodule
explanation: Hemithyroidectomy is the treatment of choice for follicular adenoma and solitary nodule[cite: 1]. Hemithyroidectomy is removal of one lobe with isthmus[cite: 1].

questionText: Most common symptom of retrosternal goiter:
explanation:
Retrosternal goiter features:
